title: Structured Streaming
subtitle: Micro-batches, triggers, state, event time, watermarks, output modes, checkpoints, exactly-once and production debugging
mantra: A stream is a table that never stops growing: the checkpoint remembers how far you got, state remembers what you need, and the watermark decides when you may forget.
objectives: You can explain Structured Streaming from first principles: unbounded table, lazy readStream, micro-batches as Spark jobs, source → transformation → sink.
You can choose and write the right trigger (default, processingTime, availableNow, once, real-time) — including the serverless rules.
You can tell stateless from stateful operators and predict state growth.
You can reason in event time: assign events to windows, compute watermarks and decide whether a late event is accepted.
You can pick append / update / complete per query and sink, and implement update-like results with foreachBatch + MERGE.
You can explain what a checkpoint stores, when it is incompatible, and exactly what exactly-once does and does not guarantee.
You can write stream-static and stream-stream joins with watermarks and explain the min watermark policy.
You can debug slow, stalled, lossy, duplicating and state-heavy streams with ordered playbooks.

sections.title: Streaming From First Principles: the Unbounded Table
sections.hook: Structured Streaming is not a different Spark — it is the same engine running over data that never ends.

blocks.text: **Batch**: the input is known now (A, B, C, D). You process it, you get a result, you **stop**. The dataset is **bounded**.
**Streaming**: at 10:00 A and B arrive, at 10:01 C, at 10:02 D and E, at 10:03 F … You don't know where it ends. The dataset is logically **unbounded**.

BATCH (bounded)            STREAMING (unbounded)
 A B C D                    10:00  A B
   │ process                10:01  C
   ▼                        10:02  D E
 result → STOP              10:03  F
                            ...    (no END)
blocks.caption: Bounded vs unbounded input

blocks.title: The unbounded table model
blocks.text: Think of a stream as a **table that keeps growing**: every new event is a new row appended at the bottom. Your query is defined once over that table; the engine runs it **incrementally** over the new rows.
Because of that model you can write streaming transformations **almost like batch DataFrames**:

blocks.code:
result = (
    stream_df
        .filter("amount > 0")
        .groupBy("country")
        .count()
)
blocks.caption: Looks like batch — runs incrementally

blocks.text: The difference is hidden in the engine: Spark keeps **execution progress** and, where needed, **intermediate state** between different arrivals of data.
The mental model of this whole chapter, top to bottom:

STREAMING SOURCE
      ↓
readStream
      ↓
incremental DataFrame plan
      ↓
trigger
      ↓
micro-batch / real-time execution
      ↓
stateless or stateful operators
      ↓
writeStream
      ↓
sink
      │
      └── checkpoint: remembers progress + state
blocks.caption: The Phase 5 mental model

blocks.title: Why can streaming reuse batch DataFrame syntax?
blocks.text: Because Structured Streaming uses Spark's **DataFrame / query-planning execution model**, applied **incrementally** over unbounded input. Same planner, same jobs/stages/tasks — just re-run on new data.

items.def: Input with a known end (yesterday's orders.csv). Process once, then stop.
Input that logically keeps growing (Kafka topic, files landing forever).
Whether the query must remember information from previous micro-batches (see section 5).
Durable storage of progress (offsets, commits) and state — the stream's memory.

blocks.title: What this chapter builds on
blocks.text: Batch vs streaming basics: Chapter 2. Partitions, skew and Spark UI: Chapter 9. Auto Loader specifics (cloudFiles, schemaLocation, file discovery): Chapter 12. Here we go **underneath** Auto Loader into the Structured Streaming engine itself.

blocks.label: Think first: is a nightly job that only processes new rows 'streaming'?
blocks.text: Not necessarily. Streaming describes an **unbounded input + incremental engine**. You'll see in section 4 that the streaming engine can even run as a scheduled job that stops (`availableNow`).

sections.title: readStream, writeStream & the Lazy Start
sections.hook: One word — readStream instead of read — changes the whole execution model.

items.title: Batch read
points: Ends when the files are read

items.title: Streaming read
points: "Treat this source as **continuously evolving** and track my progress."

blocks.code:
df = (
    spark.readStream
        .format("json")
        .schema(schema)      # streaming file sources need a schema
        .load(path)
)
blocks.caption: First streaming DataFrame

blocks.title: Trap: read vs readStream
blocks.text: `spark.read` → **bounded batch read**. `spark.readStream` → **streaming source**. Simple, but frequently tested — and calling `.writeStream` on a batch DataFrame fails.
**readStream does not start anything.** It is Spark lazy evaluation again: it only builds a streaming DataFrame / logical plan.

blocks.code:
events = spark.readStream.format(...).load(...)   # plan only

query = (
    events.writeStream
        .format("delta")
        .option("checkpointLocation", checkpoint)
        .toTable("ecommerce.bronze.events")   # <- starts the query
)
blocks.caption: Execution starts at the sink

blocks.text: `toTable(name)` starts a query that writes into a table; `start()` starts a query whose sink is given by `format(...)`/path or by `foreachBatch`. Both return a **StreamingQuery** handle.
A full stream always has three parts: **SOURCE → TRANSFORMATION → SINK**.

blocks.code:
events = spark.readStream.table("ecommerce.bronze.events")          # SOURCE

clean = events.filter("event_type IS NOT NULL")                      # TRANSFORMATION

query = (
    clean.writeStream
        .option("checkpointLocation", checkpoint)
        .toTable("ecommerce.silver.events")                         # SINK
)
blocks.caption: Source → transformation → sink, Delta to Delta

head: Handle call
What it gives you
rows: What the query is doing right now (e.g. waiting for data, trigger active?)
Metrics of the last completed micro-batch (rows, rates, durations, state, watermark)
A list of the most recent progress reports
Block until the query stops (useful in jobs/scripts)
blocks.caption: The StreamingQuery handle (monitoring in depth: section 15)

blocks.title: No checkpoint = no memory
blocks.text: Every production `writeStream` needs a durable `checkpointLocation` (e.g. a path in a Volume). It is how the query remembers progress across restarts (section 9).

blocks.label: Think first: you run a cell that only contains `events = spark.readStream...load(path)`. Does Spark read any file?
blocks.text: No. Like any transformation, it just defines a plan. Nothing executes until a streaming sink is started with `writeStream ... toTable()/start()` (or a notebook `display()` starts a query for you).

sections.title: Micro-batches & the processingTime Trigger
sections.hook: Spark doesn't launch a job per event — it groups arrivals into small batches. Every batch lesson you learned still applies.

blocks.text: Events arrive at 12:00:00 (e1), 12:00:01 (e2), 12:00:02 (e3), 12:00:03 (e4), 12:00:04 (e5). Spark doesn't need a new distributed job for each event — it **groups** them.

arrivals:  e1  e2  e3  e4  e5
           └─┬─┘   └─┬─┘   │
Micro-batch 1: e1 e2
Micro-batch 2: e3 e4
Micro-batch 3: e5
blocks.caption: Micro-batching

blocks.title: Micro-batch = a small Spark job
blocks.text: A **micro-batch** is a bounded chunk of newly available stream data, executed as a Spark job. new input → micro-batch N → job → stages → tasks → partitions.
So everything from Chapter 9 still applies inside every batch: **job, stage, task, partition, shuffle, join, spill, skew**.

blocks.code:
query = (
    events.writeStream
        .format("delta")
        .outputMode("append")
        .option("checkpointLocation", checkpoint)
        .trigger(processingTime="5 seconds")
        .toTable("ecommerce.bronze.events")
)
blocks.caption: 5-second micro-batches (classic compute)

blocks.text:
00–05 s  → batch 0
05–10 s  → batch 1
10–15 s  → batch 2
blocks.caption: Conceptually, with a 5-second trigger

blocks.text: The **processingTime** trigger says **how often** Spark tries to start a new micro-batch. It is a schedule for attempts, not a promise of completion.

blocks.label: Think first: the trigger is every 5 seconds, but one micro-batch needs 12 seconds. Does Spark run three batches in parallel to keep up?
blocks.text: No. In the normal sequential micro-batch model, batch 2 starts only **after** batch 1 finishes (0 → 12 s, then the next). A **processing backlog** builds up and latency grows.

trigger = every 5 s, batch needs 12 s
Batch 1: |0 ──────────── 12|
Batch 2:                   |12 ──────────── 24|
Batch 3:                                      |24 → ...
→ backlog grows, end-to-end latency grows
blocks.caption: Batches never overlap

blocks.title: Production signal
blocks.text: Batches consistently longer than the trigger interval mean **ingestion rate > processing capacity**. The trigger can't fix that — only more capacity or a cheaper query can (section 14).

blocks.title: Ask yourself when batches overrun the trigger
questions: Is the batch duration consistently above the trigger interval, or was it one spike?
Is the input rate growing, or is the same input taking longer each batch?
Which stage inside the slow micro-batch dominates (shuffle, skew, state, sink)?

sections.title: Trigger Types: Default, AvailableNow, Once, Real-time & Serverless
sections.hook: The trigger decides WHEN batches run — including 'catch up, then stop', which is the Data Engineer's favourite.

head: Trigger
Syntax
Meaning
rows: Start the next micro-batch as soon as the previous one finishes
Old 'one batch then stop' — replaced by AvailableNow
blocks.caption: Today's important trigger models

blocks.title: Once is deprecated
blocks.text: Databricks deprecated `Trigger.Once` in favour of `Trigger.AvailableNow`. Once processes the backlog in a single batch; AvailableNow can split it into several batches (respecting rate limits) and still stops at the end.
**AvailableNow** in practice: every hour you want *'process all new records since last time, then stop'*.

blocks.code:
query = (
    events.writeStream
        .trigger(availableNow=True)
        .option("checkpointLocation", checkpoint)
        .toTable("ecommerce.bronze.events")
)
blocks.caption: Scheduled incremental processing

blocks.text:
Run 1:  available: A B C   → process A B C → stop
         (checkpoint now knows A B C)
1 hour later
Run 2:  available: D E     → process D E   → stop
blocks.caption: AvailableNow + checkpoint = incremental batch

blocks.title: Streaming ≠ always-on
blocks.text: The streaming engine can power **scheduled incremental batch** jobs. Databricks especially recommends AvailableNow for **serverless jobs**.

Why use the streaming engine for scheduled batch? You get **incremental source tracking, checkpointing, state management, fault recovery and incremental semantics** for free — instead of hand-writing:

blocks.code:
last_processed_timestamp = ...          # stored where? updated when?
df = spark.sql(f"SELECT * FROM src WHERE event_ts > '{last_processed_timestamp}'")
blocks.caption: The manual progress tracking AvailableNow replaces

blocks.text: This is exactly the model Auto Loader uses (Chapter 12): a streaming source + checkpoint + AvailableNow on a schedule.

**Real-time mode** (classic Databricks) targets **sub-second end-to-end latency** for ultra-low-latency operational workloads in supported scenarios. It is **not** the default choice for ordinary lakehouse ETL — micro-batch or AvailableNow is simpler, cheaper and easier to operate.

blocks.title: Trap: serverless + always-on
blocks.text: On serverless notebooks/jobs, time-based `processingTime` triggers aren't supported. For **always-running** serverless streams, the preferred architecture is a **Lakeflow pipeline in continuous mode** (Phase 6).

blocks.title: Trap: AvailableNow
blocks.text: AvailableNow = **process the currently available backlog incrementally, then stop**. Not 'run forever', and not 'reprocess everything'.

blocks.label: Think first: you run an AvailableNow query twice in a row with no new data. What does run 2 process?
blocks.text: Nothing new — the checkpoint already records that all available input was processed, so the query finds no new offsets and stops.

sections.title: Stateless vs Stateful & the State Store
sections.hook: Can each record be handled alone, or must Spark remember the past? That one question decides cost, risk and recovery.

blocks.code:
clean = (
    events
        .filter("amount > 0")
        .select("event_id", "customer_id", "amount")
)
blocks.caption: Stateless

blocks.text: For every record you can decide what to do **without remembering previous records**: event → filter → projection → output. Databricks defines **stateless** queries as queries that keep no intermediate state beyond **progress tracking** from source to sink.

blocks.code: events.groupBy("customer_id").count()
blocks.caption: Stateful

blocks.text: To answer *'customer 42 count = ?'* Spark must remember: batch 1 → customer 42 = 5; batch 2 brings 3 more → new total = 8. That memory is **state**.

items.title: Stateful
points: State saved in the checkpoint → harder to change

blocks.title: What state really is
blocks.text: **State** = information from previous micro-batches needed to correctly process the next ones. It is not the final output — it is the **working memory** of the streaming computation.
**Why state can explode**: `groupBy("customer_id").count()` with 1 million new customers per day and no reason to ever forget old ones.

blocks.title: Unbounded state
blocks.text: A stateful query without a time bound keeps every key forever. That is why **watermarks** (section 7) are so important.

**The state store.** Streaming state is not a Python dictionary on the driver. It is **distributed state** attached to the stateful operators, partitioned across executors and made durable via the checkpoint.
For demanding stateful workloads Databricks currently recommends the **RocksDB state store with changelog checkpointing**: it scales state better and reduces state-checkpoint overhead and latency.

blocks.code:
spark.conf.set(
  "spark.sql.streaming.stateStore.providerClass",
  "com.databricks.sql.streaming.state.RocksDBStateStoreProvider")
spark.conf.set(
  "spark.sql.streaming.stateStore.rocksdb.changelogCheckpointing.enabled", "true")
blocks.caption: Reference only — don't configure blindly; recognise when state is the bottleneck

blocks.title: State bottleneck ≠ compute bottleneck
blocks.text: When **state** becomes the bottleneck, bigger compute alone isn't necessarily the fix — the state design (watermark, keys) and the **state-store architecture** may matter more. You don't need RocksDB internals yet.

blocks.title: Ask yourself when the state store is huge
questions: How many keys does state hold — is key cardinality unbounded?
Is there a watermark, and is it much longer than real lateness?
How long are my windows?
Do my stream-stream joins have time bounds, and what is my dedup horizon?
Is one stateful key (e.g. 'anonymous') skewed?
Is this really a compute problem — or is the state semantically unbounded?

blocks.label: Think first: is `groupBy(...).count()` stateful in batch Spark too?
blocks.text: In a batch job it simply computes once and forgets. In **streaming**, yes — the aggregate must accumulate across micro-batches, so Spark keeps state between them.

sections.title: Event Time vs Processing Time & Event-time Windows
sections.hook: An order placed at 10:03 that arrives at 10:11 still belongs to 10:00–10:10. Which clock you use decides correctness.

blocks.text: Why can they differ? A **mobile** client offline, **network delay**, a **Kafka backlog**, a **server outage**, **retries**, a **batch upload**, **clock skew**. The purchase happened at 10:03 but arrived at 10:11 → the record is **late-arriving**.

blocks.title: Trap: processing time vs event time
blocks.text: Processing time = when Databricks processes it. Event time = the timestamp of when the event occurred. **Watermarks use event time**, not the arrival wall clock.
**Event-time windows**: sales per 10-minute window.

blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

sales = (
    events
        .groupBy(F.window("event_time", "10 minutes"))
        .agg(F.sum("amount").alias("revenue"))
)
blocks.caption: Tumbling 10-minute windows
The window is chosen by event time

blocks.title: Tumbling vs sliding windows
blocks.text: `F.window(col, "10 minutes")` = **tumbling**: fixed, non-overlapping, each event in exactly one window. `F.window(col, "10 minutes", "5 minutes")` = **sliding** (window 10 min, slide 5 min): windows overlap, so each event lands in window/slide = **2** windows. (Sliding windows are standard Spark API, added here for completeness.)
The window column is a struct with `window.start` and `window.end` — you'll use `window.start` later as a MERGE key (section 13).
**The late-data problem.** At 10:10 you might say *'window 10:00–10:10 is finished'*. But at 10:15 an event with `event_time = 10:08` arrives — it belongs to the old window.
We need a compromise → the **watermark**.

blocks.label: Think first: with 10-minute tumbling windows, which window does an event with event_time 10:19:59 land in — and one with 10:20:00?

sections.title: Watermarks: Bounding State & Late Data
sections.hook: The watermark is the deal you make: 'I'll keep state for events up to X late — older ones I may drop.'

blocks.code:
watermarked = (
    events
        .withWatermark("event_time", "10 minutes")
)

blocks.text: Meaning, approximately: *I'm willing to keep state so I can accept events that arrive up to about 10 minutes late **relative to the event-time progress I have observed**.*
Databricks defines a **watermark** as an event-time threshold that lets Structured Streaming **stop keeping old state** and **control late-arriving data**.

blocks.title: Watermark ≠ wall-clock timer
blocks.text: It does NOT mean 'each event gets 10 real minutes from its birth'. Spark tracks the **maximum event time seen** and computes: watermark ≈ max event time − delay. Max seen 12:00, delay 10 min → watermark ≈ **11:50**. State older than that may be considered final/evictable.

event-time axis ───────────────────────────────►
            11:50                   12:00
              │◄──── delay 10 min ────►│
          watermark               max event time seen
 older than watermark → too late (may be dropped)
 newer than watermark → still accepted
blocks.caption: Watermark = max event time − delay

blocks.text: Why 'approximately'? The API guarantees the actual watermark stays **at least** the configured delay behind event-time progress; coordination between partitions (and, in micro-batch mode, the watermark being updated at the end of a batch and applied to the next) means you must not treat its instantaneous value as a perfect wall-clock cutoff.

blocks.title: One-liner
blocks.text: *Watermark is an event-time progress threshold, not a simple timer per row.*

blocks.title: The guarantee in one line
blocks.text: Data **less late** than the delay is guaranteed to be aggregated. Data **later** than the threshold **may** be dropped — 'may', not 'will': don't build logic that relies on late rows being discarded.

blocks.code:
sales = (
    events
        .withWatermark("event_time", "15 minutes")
        .groupBy(
            F.window("event_time", "10 minutes"),
            F.col("country"))
        .agg(F.sum("amount").alias("revenue"))
)
blocks.caption: Stateful aggregation with a watermark

blocks.text: When the watermark passes sufficiently beyond an old window, that window's **state can be removed** → state stays **bounded**.

items.title: Short watermark (5 min)
points: ❌ records later than the tolerance may be dropped

blocks.title: Too small drops valid data
blocks.text: Databricks describes exactly this **latency / state / correctness** trade-off and warns that a very small watermark can discard **valid** late records. Pick it from how late real data actually arrives.

blocks.title: Trap: watermark purpose
blocks.text: Correct: **bound state + define tolerated lateness / finalization**. Wrong: 'delete old table rows'. A watermark is **not a retention policy** — not VACUUM, not table retention, not a TTL. It never deletes historical Delta rows.

**'Late' is relative to query progress.** An event arrives 20 minutes after it happened. Late? If the stream's max seen event time is only 5 minutes ahead of it → **could still be accepted**. If the stream has already seen events 2 hours ahead → **could be too late**.

blocks.title: late ≠ now − event_time
blocks.text: Lateness depends on **event-time watermark progress**, not on how long the event spent in transit.

blocks.title: Ask yourself when late events seem to be missing
questions: What event_time did the missing events carry?
What was the maximum event time already observed when they arrived?
What watermark delay was configured?
Had the watermark already passed their window?
Am I reasoning from arrival time instead of event time?

blocks.label: Think first: max event time seen = 10:20, watermark delay 5 min. An event with event_time 10:03 arrives. Accepted? What if the delay were 30 min?
blocks.text: 5 min → watermark ≈ 10:15 > 10:03 → **too late**, may be dropped. 30 min → watermark ≈ 09:50 < 10:03 → **still accepted** and updates its window's state.

sections.title: Output Modes: Append, Update, Complete
sections.hook: When a result can still change, which rows do you emit — the final ones, the changed ones, or everything?

head: Mode
What it emits each trigger
rows: Only rows considered **final** (will never change again)
Rows whose result **changed** in this trigger

blocks.text: **Append**: the 10:00–10:10 revenue may still change at 10:11 because of late data, so append must not emit it yet. With a watermark: wait until the window is considered final → **emit once**. For window aggregations, append writes after the watermark passes the window.
**Update**: batch 1 → GR revenue = 100 → emit `GR 100`. Batch 2 receives +50 → GR = 150 → emit `GR 150`. Downstream sees **updates**.
**Complete**: every trigger emits the whole aggregate. Batch 1: GR 100, DE 50. Batch 2: GR 150, DE 50, FR 20 — all of it rewritten.

blocks.title: Complete mode keeps all state
blocks.text: In complete mode aggregation state is **not evicted by the watermark** (the whole result must be re-emitted). With large/unbounded key cardinality it gets expensive.

blocks.title: Delta sink: append + complete, NOT update
blocks.text: Delta Lake streaming sinks support **append** and **complete**, not **update** directly. For update-like semantics into Delta use **foreachBatch + MERGE** (section 13). A classic certification/interview detail.

**Stateless streams**: `events.filter(...).select(...)` has no stateful row that changes later, so the append/update/complete distinction doesn't change operator behaviour (and complete mode isn't allowed without an aggregation).
**Production example — event analytics.** Schema: `event_id STRING, user_id BIGINT, event_type STRING, event_time TIMESTAMP`.

blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

events = spark.readStream.table("ecommerce.bronze.events")

counts = (
    events
        .withWatermark("event_time", "20 minutes")
        .groupBy(F.window("event_time", "5 minutes"), "event_type")
        .count()
)

query = (
    counts.writeStream
        .outputMode("append")
        .option("checkpointLocation",
                "/Volumes/ecommerce/system/event_counts_ckpt")
        .toTable("ecommerce.gold.event_counts")
)
blocks.caption: Window + watermark + append → Delta

blocks.text:
events 10:01 click, 10:02 click, 10:03 purchase
   → window [10:00–10:05) state: click=2, purchase=1
late event, event_time 10:04 → state updates
watermark advances past 10:05 (max event time ≥ ~10:25)
   → append: window FINAL → emit row once
   → window state removed
blocks.caption: The complete lifecycle of one window

blocks.title: "Why does append output look delayed?"
blocks.text: Events arrive instantly but rows don't appear. **Stateful aggregate + append mode + watermark** means Spark must wait until it considers the aggregate final (window end + watermark delay). This is **intended behaviour**, not necessarily lag.

blocks.title: Trap: output mode
blocks.text: Append = finalized rows. Update = changed rows. Complete = entire result. And **not every sink supports every mode** — Delta doesn't support update directly.

blocks.label: Think first: a dashboard must show click counts growing live (10:01 → 1, 10:02 → 2) in a Delta table. Which output mode?
blocks.text: Not append (waits for finality) and not update (Delta sink doesn't support it). Use **foreachBatch + MERGE** to upsert the changing aggregates (section 13).

sections.title: Checkpoint Internals: Offsets, Commits, State & Query Identity
sections.hook: In Chapter 2 the checkpoint was 'where I stopped'. Now we open the box — and see why it is part of the query's identity.

blocks.text: The Databricks docs say a checkpoint directory contains at least **offsets**, **commits** and, for stateful workloads, **state** metadata/content.

checkpoint/
│
├── offsets/    what range each micro-batch READS
├── commits/    which micro-batches were WRITTEN to the sink
├── state/      state-store data of stateful operators
└── metadata    the query's identity
blocks.caption: Inside a checkpoint

items.def: The source's 'how far have I read?'. Kafka: partition 0 → offset 1050, partition 1 → offset 2040. File/Auto Loader sources have an equivalent progress concept.
Record of the micro-batches that have successfully committed to the sink — a key part of exactly-once semantics.
State-store metadata/content for stateful operators (counts per customer, open windows, join buffers, dedup keys).
Identifies the query; changing it effectively means a different query.

blocks.text: **Offsets**: the checkpoint keeps the source offsets / progress for **each micro-batch**. **Commits**: suppose micro-batch 42 processed source range X — the checkpoint must also know *'was batch 42 written successfully to the sink?'*.

**State in the checkpoint**: for `events.groupBy("customer_id").count()`, after a restart Spark must remember customer_1 = 120, customer_2 = 50 … Without it, a new event for customer_1 wouldn't know the previous total was 120.

blocks.title: Trap: what a checkpoint stores
blocks.text: Progress **offsets**, **commits** and **state** information (plus query metadata) — **not** just a 'last timestamp'.

**Why stateful queries are harder to change.** The checkpoint's state has a schema: key = customer_id, value = count. Change the code to key = country, value = sum(amount) and you can't necessarily reuse the same checkpoint. Databricks has explicit restrictions on what may change between restarts from the same checkpoint.

blocks.title: A checkpoint is not a generic reusable folder
blocks.text: It encodes the **query identity and state**. One checkpoint ↔ one query. Never share it between two streams.
**Deleting the checkpoint** (or changing `checkpointLocation`) makes the next run start as a **new query**: query identity, progress and state are gone.

blocks.caption: What a lost checkpoint can mean (per pipeline)

head: Change between deployments
Checkpoint reuse
rows: Often OK — depends on the exact query
blocks.caption: Checkpoint & code deployment

blocks.title: Rule for deployments
blocks.text: Never assume 'same checkpoint' means 'new code will pick up seamlessly'. Consult the compatibility rules and **test stateful deployments** carefully.

**Stateful restart from a new checkpoint.** If you change the state architecture, the old checkpoint is incompatible and you may need **new checkpoint + full recomputation/backfill**. That is expensive — which is why **state schema is effectively production data**.

blocks.title: Ask yourself before deploying a change to a streaming query
questions: Is this query stateless or stateful?
Does my change touch state keys, state schema, the source type or the stateful operators?
If the checkpoint becomes incompatible, can I afford a new checkpoint + backfill?
Have I tested the restart from the existing checkpoint in a non-prod copy?

blocks.title: Sandbox lab: checkpoint reset
blocks.text: Run a stream, then restart it with a **new checkpoint location**: it behaves as a brand-new stream. That proves the checkpoint is part of query identity. **Only in a sandbox** — never casually in production.

blocks.label: Think first: you delete the checkpoint of an append Bronze→Silver stream reading a Delta table and restart. What do you expect in Silver?
blocks.text: The query starts as new, so it re-reads the source from its starting point and **re-appends rows already written → duplicates** (and any stateful results restart from zero).

sections.title: Exactly-once: What It Really Means (and Streaming Dedup)
sections.hook: Exactly-once is a precise engine guarantee with sharp edges — not a promise that duplicates can't exist.

blocks.text: For a managed **Delta streaming sink**, three things cooperate so that a retried micro-batch never becomes a partial or duplicate commit:
Databricks states the Delta streaming sink provides **exactly-once processing guarantees**, even with concurrent streams or batch queries on the table.
**Failure scenario**: micro-batch 20 reads events 1000–1100 and writes to Delta. The system crashes exactly at the boundary. On restart the engine must decide: *was batch 20 committed?*

1. write offsets/20  (plan: read 1000–1100)
2. process batch 20
3. Delta commit (tagged with query id + batch 20)
4. write commits/20
        ✗ crash somewhere
restart: offsets/20 exists, commits/20 missing
  → batch 20 already in the Delta log?  skip it
  → not in the log?                     retry it
NEVER: "half applied twice"
blocks.caption: Restart decision

blocks.title: Exactly-once stops at the boundaries
blocks.text: `foreachBatch(send_email)` sends 100 emails, then the process crashes before the checkpoint commit. On retry the same batch runs again → **emails sent again**. The email service has no Delta transaction semantics. Structured Streaming exactly-once ≠ every arbitrary side effect exactly once.
Databricks stresses that exactly-once guarantees in managed Delta flows **stop at the edges** — custom or non-transactional sinks. There you must make the write **idempotent**.

blocks.title: Exactly-once ≠ no duplicate source events
blocks.text: Kafka can deliver `event_id=123` twice as **two distinct records**. The engine processes each input record exactly once — and both duplicates land in the table. **Processing guarantee ≠ business deduplication** (same lesson as Auto Loader files, Chapter 12).
**Streaming deduplication.** The simple version:

blocks.code: unique = events.dropDuplicates(["event_id"])
blocks.caption: Correct result — unbounded state

blocks.text: Problem: to know whether `event_id=123` has **ever** appeared, Spark must remember every event ID **forever** → unbounded state. You usually need a **watermark / time bound**:

blocks.code:
unique = (
    events
        .withWatermark("event_time", "1 hour")
        .dropDuplicates(["event_id", "event_time"])
)
blocks.caption: Dedup state cleaned as event time progresses

blocks.text: Including the watermarked `event_time` column in the dedup keys lets Spark drop old keys once the watermark passes them. **Deduplication is a stateful operation.**

blocks.title: dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark
blocks.text: Newer Spark/Databricks runtimes also offer `events.withWatermark("event_time", "1 hour").dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark(["event_id"])` — dedups on the key alone for duplicates arriving within the watermark delay, even if their timestamps differ slightly. (Standard API, beyond the source; the source's pattern above is the classic one.)

blocks.title: Ask yourself when someone says 'it's exactly-once, so no duplicates'
questions: Is the sink a managed Delta sink, or a custom / foreachBatch / external sink?
Could the source itself contain the same business event twice?
Was the checkpoint ever reset or changed?
Is there any non-idempotent side effect (emails, API calls, balance += x)?

blocks.label: Think first: Q18 — 'Exactly-once Delta sink means the source cannot contain duplicates.' True?
blocks.text: **No.** Processing guarantees don't deduplicate semantically duplicated input records. Two records with the same event_id are two records to the engine.

sections.title: Streaming Joins: Stream-Static & Stream-Stream
sections.hook: Joining a live stream to a table is easy; joining two live streams forces Spark to wait — and waiting costs state.

blocks.text: **Stream-static join**: live `orders` stream + a relatively static `products` table. Very common for enrichment.

blocks.code:
products = spark.table("ecommerce.silver.products")   # static (batch) side

enriched = (
    orders_stream
        .join(products, "product_id")
)
blocks.caption: stream events + static dimension → enriched stream

blocks.title: Static side semantics
blocks.text: If the static table changes, behaviour depends on the query/execution semantics and refresh architecture. With a Delta static side, **new** micro-batches may join against a newer version — but a long-running stream does **not** magically recompute already-written outputs because a dimension changed. If correctness requires recomputation when dimensions change, materialized/declarative pipeline patterns (Phase 6) may fit better.

**Stream-stream join**: `orders` stream + `payments` stream, matched on `order_id`. The order event arrives at 10:00, the payment at 10:02 → Spark must keep the **order in state** until its payment arrives. For how long? Forever? Without a watermark/time condition, state can grow **without bound**.

blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

orders_w   = orders.withWatermark("order_time", "30 minutes")
payments_w = payments.withWatermark("payment_time", "30 minutes")

joined = orders_w.alias("o").join(
    payments_w.alias("p"),
    F.expr("""
        o.order_id = p.order_id AND
        p.payment_time BETWEEN o.order_time
                           AND o.order_time + INTERVAL 1 HOUR
    """),
    "inner")
blocks.caption: Key + time relationship + watermarks on both sides

blocks.text: The join condition contains **key + time relationship**: same `order_id` **and** the payment occurs within the expected time range. Databricks recommends **watermarks on both inputs** so obsolete state can be discarded.

blocks.title: Trap: watermarks and outer joins
blocks.text: For stream-stream **outer** joins a watermark (plus a time constraint) is **required**: the engine must know when an unmatched record can be considered final and emitted with NULLs.

**Multiple watermarks.** orders: 10 min delay, payments: 1 hour delay. Spark must compute **one global watermark**. The default policy is **min** — the slowest stream decides progress. You can choose **max**, but then records of the slower stream may be dropped; Databricks warns to use it with care.

blocks.code:
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.streaming.multipleWatermarkPolicy", "min")   # default
# "max" = faster progress, but slow-stream records may be dropped
blocks.caption: The policy setting

blocks.text:
orders watermark   → 14:00
payments watermark → 13:00
policy max: global 14:00 → state for 13:xx may be dropped
            but payments for 13:xx can still arrive  ✗
policy min: global 13:00 → follows the SLOWEST input  ✓
blocks.caption: Why 'min' protects correctness

blocks.title: Ask yourself before writing a stream-stream join
questions: How long can a matching record from the other stream arrive after this one?
Do both inputs have a watermark on their event-time column?
Does my join condition include a time range, not just the key?
Is it an outer join (then watermark + time constraint are mandatory)?
Will the global watermark (min) be held back by a slow input?

blocks.label: Think first: why do stream-stream joins need state at all, when stream-static joins don't buffer the stream?
blocks.text: Because a record from one stream may need to **wait** for a later matching record from the other stream. The static side is fully available every batch; a stream side isn't.

sections.title: Delta as Streaming Source & Sink: Changes and Retention
sections.hook: Delta-to-Delta streaming is the backbone of medallion pipelines — with two operational landmines.

blocks.code: bronze = spark.readStream.table("ecommerce.bronze.events")
blocks.caption: Stream the additions of a Bronze Delta table downstream

blocks.text: Delta tables can be both **sources** and **sinks** of Structured Streaming. A Bronze table that keeps receiving rows can feed Silver incrementally.

blocks.title: Delta source is append-oriented
blocks.text: A simple Delta streaming source naturally streams **appends**. If the source table gets **UPDATE / DELETE / MERGE**, downstream semantics need more care. For row-level changes, **Change Data Feed** is often the right tool (joined with CDC later).

Accuracy note (standard Delta behaviour): by default a commit that changes existing data in the source makes the stream **fail** rather than silently re-emit rewritten files. The option `skipChangeCommits` ignores such commits (their changes are **not** propagated); reading the **Change Data Feed** propagates them properly.

blocks.code:
# ignore update/delete commits (changes NOT propagated)
spark.readStream.option("skipChangeCommits", "true").table("ecommerce.bronze.events")

# propagate row-level changes via Change Data Feed
spark.readStream.option("readChangeFeed", "true").table("ecommerce.silver.customers")
blocks.caption: Two ways to handle non-append source commits

blocks.text: **Source retention caveat.** If a stream reading a Delta source is stopped much longer than the source's retention, the files/history it needs may be **vacuumed** — it may never catch up.

Friday:        stream stops (checkpoint: "I need version X")
source:        VACUUM retention = 7 days
2 weeks later: restart
               version X files no longer exist
→ stream cannot recover incrementally
blocks.caption: Retention vs a stopped stream

blocks.title: Run at least once per retention window
blocks.text: Databricks: a stream must run **at least once within the source retention window**, otherwise it may fail with a **missing-file** error and need a reset/full refresh. Design streaming operations and source retention **together**.

blocks.title: Don't 'fix' missing files with ignoreMissingFiles
blocks.text: Do **not** set `spark.sql.files.ignoreMissingFiles=true` as a workaround for a stream that fell behind Delta retention — Databricks warns it can produce **silent incorrect results**. Correct fix: **increase retention**, or **recover/rebuild** the stream appropriately. Never suppress a correctness error.

blocks.caption: Increasing retention so a stopped stream can still catch up

blocks.title: Ask yourself when a Delta-source stream fails after a long stop
questions: How long was the stream stopped, compared with the source's retention settings?
Did a VACUUM run on the source in the meantime (DESCRIBE HISTORY)?
Is the error about missing files for a version the checkpoint still needs?
Am I tempted to flip ignoreMissingFiles — and do I understand that hides data loss?

blocks.label: Think first: Q28 — why can a stream fail if it was stopped beyond Delta retention?
blocks.text: Because the source versions/files it still needs to read were **vacuumed** before the stream caught up. The checkpoint points to data that physically no longer exists.

sections.title: foreachBatch, Streaming MERGE & Idempotency
sections.hook: foreachBatch turns each micro-batch into an ordinary DataFrame — full power, full responsibility.

blocks.code:
def process_batch(batch_df, batch_id):
    ...

query = (
    stream_df.writeStream
        .foreachBatch(process_batch)
        .option("checkpointLocation", checkpoint)
        .start()
)
blocks.caption: The bridge between streaming and batch APIs

blocks.text: Inside the function you can use **batch-only** operations: **MERGE**, complex Delta DML, custom sink logic.

blocks.code:
from delta.tables import DeltaTable

def upsert(batch_df, batch_id):
    target = DeltaTable.forName(spark, "ecommerce.silver.customers")
    (target.alias("t")
        .merge(batch_df.alias("s"), "t.customer_id = s.customer_id")
        .whenMatchedUpdateAll()
        .whenNotMatchedInsertAll()
        .execute())

query = (
    changes.writeStream
        .foreachBatch(upsert)
        .option("checkpointLocation", checkpoint)
        .start()
)
blocks.caption: The classic streaming-upsert pattern

blocks.title: foreachBatch must be idempotent
blocks.text: If batch 10 retries, your function **may execute again**. `balance = balance + incoming_amount` twice → wrong. `MERGE` by a stable business key/version → can be idempotent. foreachBatch gives power, but **you** become responsible for sink-side idempotency.

items.title: Idempotent
points: Upsert where replay gives the same end state

blocks.text: **batch_id** can help some external-sink patterns recognise a **replayed** batch. But don't treat batch_id alone as a universal business dedup key — the safest design depends on the target system.

blocks.title: Delta's built-in idempotent foreachBatch writes
blocks.text: For plain Delta writes inside foreachBatch, Delta supports the writer options `txnAppId` (a stable id for the query) and `txnVersion` (e.g. the batch_id) so a replayed batch is skipped. (Standard Delta API, beyond the source.)

**Update-like results to Delta.** A dashboard wants live counts (10:01 → click_count=1, 10:02 → 2). Delta doesn't support streaming update output mode as a sink, so implement update-like semantics with foreachBatch + MERGE:

blocks.code:
def merge_counts(batch_df, batch_id):
    target = DeltaTable.forName(spark, "ecommerce.gold.live_event_counts")
    (target.alias("t")
        .merge(batch_df.alias("s"),
               """t.window_start = s.window.start
                  AND t.event_type = s.event_type""")
        .whenMatchedUpdateAll()
        .whenNotMatchedInsertAll()
        .execute())

(counts.writeStream
    .outputMode("update")          # emit changed aggregates to the function
    .foreachBatch(merge_counts)
    .option("checkpointLocation", ckpt)
    .start())
blocks.caption: Window aggregates upserted into Delta

blocks.title: Why update mode is fine here
blocks.text: The **sink** is now your function, not the Delta sink — so `outputMode("update")` simply hands each batch's **changed** aggregate rows to the function, which MERGEs them. (In practice flatten `window.start` into a real `window_start` column to match the target schema.)

blocks.title: Ask yourself before shipping a foreachBatch function
questions: If this exact batch runs twice, is the end state the same?
Am I merging on a stable business key (and version/sequence)?
Do I trigger external side effects that can't be rolled back?
Can the micro-batch contain several rows per key that must be deduplicated before MERGE?

blocks.label: Think first: Q20 — why can foreachBatch duplicate external side effects even though the stream is 'exactly-once'?
blocks.text: A failed/retried batch may invoke the function again, and external sinks don't participate in Spark/Delta transaction semantics. Solution (Q21): make side effects **idempotent** — business key/version, or transactional sink semantics.

sections.title: Performance: Latency, Throughput, Backlog, Small Files & Skew
sections.hook: A stream must not only be correct — every micro-batch must finish fast enough to keep up with arrivals.

blocks.text: **Small files in streaming**: every tiny micro-batch writing to Delta → batch 1 → 2 MB file, batch 2 → 3 MB, batch 3 → 1 MB … → **small-file pressure**.

blocks.title: Physical maintenance still matters
blocks.text: Delta can compact later (**OPTIMIZE**, **predictive optimization**), and Delta's streaming integration addresses transactional and small-file concerns — but choose the latency requirement sensibly. Don't trigger every second if every minute is enough.
**Backpressure / backlog**: the source produces **50 MB/s**, the pipeline processes **20 MB/s** → **+30 MB/s** backlog.

blocks.title: No checkpoint magic fixes throughput
blocks.text: A checkpoint preserves correctness/progress; it does not create processing capacity. Sustained input > processing → latency ↑, backlog ↑, and eventually **source retention may be exceeded**.

**Micro-batch = Spark job**, so it suffers the exact same issues as batch: skew, shuffle, bad joins, too few or too many partitions, spill, executor OOM, driver OOM. Streaming adds one more dimension: **it must finish fast enough to keep up**.

trigger intended: 5 s
99 partitions → finish in 2 s
 1 partition  → takes 30 s   (skew)
→ every micro-batch ≥ 30 s → backlog grows
blocks.caption: Skew in a stream (Phase 1 meets Phase 5)

blocks.text: **Stateful + skew is especially bad.** One key `user_id = "anonymous"` holds 70% of events; `.groupBy("user_id")` creates a **hot state partition**.

blocks.title: Key design matters in streaming
blocks.text: Streaming partition/key design decides whether state is spread evenly. A hot key in state hurts every single micro-batch, forever.

blocks.title: Ask yourself when a stream can't keep up
questions: Is input rate permanently higher than processing rate, or was it a burst?
Is one task (or one state partition) much slower than the rest?
Is my trigger so small that overhead and tiny files dominate?
Will the backlog outlive the source's retention?

blocks.label: Think first: Q31 — input rate permanently exceeds processing rate. Would a checkpoint fix this?
blocks.text: No. Checkpoint preserves correctness/progress; it doesn't create processing capacity. Backlog and latency keep growing (Q30) until you add capacity or make the query cheaper.

blocks.text: input 50,000 rows/s, processed 100,000 rows/s → capacity to spare. input 100,000, processed 40,000 **sustained** → backlog grows. Often more useful than staring at cluster CPU.

**State growth**: batch durations go 10 s → 12 s → 20 s → 40 s → 2 min … while input rate is **stable**. Inspect the stateful operators: is `numRowsTotal` in state increasing forever? Likely: **missing watermark, watermark too long, unbounded key cardinality, bad stateful join**.

blocks.title: Streaming adds three factors
blocks.text: Streaming adds **state**, **source** and **sink** factors on top of ordinary Spark performance (shuffle, skew, spill, join).

First things to check

blocks.title: Ask yourself when the stream stopped making progress
questions: Is the query active, or did it terminate with an exception?
Is the source still producing — are new offsets/files available?
Is the checkpoint corrupted or changed?
Is the sink blocked, or a state batch stuck?
Did an executor fail repeatedly?
Did a permission/credential expire?
Was source retention violated while it was stopped?

blocks.title: Ask yourself when batch durations grow but input is stable
questions: Is state (numRowsTotal) growing every batch?
Is checkpoint/state-store overhead rising?
Are small output files or source metadata growth adding per-batch cost?
Is the sink slowing down?

blocks.title: Don't restart blindly
blocks.text: When a stream stops progressing, **inspect progress before restarting**. A restart can hide the evidence (and with a changed checkpoint, create duplicates).

blocks.title: Missing late records: don't blame the checkpoint first
blocks.text: Check the event-time chain (event_time → max observed → watermark → output mode → window boundaries). Blame the **checkpoint** only if evidence points there.

blocks.title: State store huge: maybe not a compute problem
blocks.text: The fix isn't necessarily bigger compute — maybe the state is **semantically unbounded** (no watermark, no join time bound, infinite dedup horizon).

blocks.title: Exactly-once is end-to-end only when every piece participates
blocks.text: Duplicates after a failure mean some piece didn't participate: a non-transactional sink, a non-idempotent foreachBatch, a duplicating source or a reset checkpoint.

blocks.title: Ask yourself when a stream is slow (the tree, as questions)
questions: Is the input backlog actually growing (input rate vs processed rate)?
Which micro-batch is slow, and since when?
Inside that batch, which stage/task dominates?
Is it a Spark problem (shuffle, skew, spill, join)?
Is it a state problem (growth, watermark, state store)?
Is it a source/sink problem (throughput, API latency, storage)?

**Lab 7 — late data**: controlled events, arrival order 10:01 (event_time 10:01), 10:02 (10:02), 10:20 (event_time 10:03). Try watermark = 5 min and = 30 min and observe whether the late record can still affect state.

blocks.title: Make Lab 7 actually show the difference
blocks.text: With only those three events, the max event time seen is **10:02**, so the 10:03 event isn't late in event-time terms under either watermark — it arrived 18 minutes late on the wall clock, but lateness is relative to event-time progress. Add an on-time event with event_time ≈ 10:20 **before** it (and let a micro-batch pass so the watermark advances): then 5 min → watermark ≈ 10:15 → dropped; 30 min → ≈ 09:50 → accepted.

Ask
rows: How late can valid records arrive?
When can old state safely disappear?
How much latency do we need?

blocks.text: Late-data tolerance sets the watermark, which bounds the state, which drives cost; the trigger sets latency and file sizes; retention must exceed your longest possible stop. Change one, re-check the others. Memory hook: **S-E-L-S-W-T-S-C-R** ("**S**treams **E**at **L**ate **S**tate, **W**atch **T**he **S**ink, **C**heck **R**etention").

items: a prolonged stop that approaches source retention

blocks.title: Q35 — How would you explain Structured Streaming?
blocks.text: Structured Streaming treats an unbounded data source as an **incrementally growing table**. You define transformations with Spark's DataFrame model; the engine executes newly available data in **micro-batches** or supported low-latency modes. **Checkpoints** track source progress and commits, **state stores** preserve intermediate state for aggregations, joins and deduplication, and **watermarks** bound that state and define lateness tolerance for event-time processing.

blocks.label: Think first: in the mini-project, why is Bronze→Silver fine with AvailableNow and no watermark, while Silver→Gold needs one?
blocks.text: Bronze→Silver is **stateless** (filters) — only progress is tracked. Silver→Gold is a **windowed aggregation in append mode**: without a watermark the windows could never be finalized (append isn't even allowed) and state would grow forever.

pitfalls.title: read instead of readStream
pitfalls.text: `spark.read` builds a bounded batch DataFrame; calling `.writeStream` on it fails.
pitfalls.fix: Use `spark.readStream` for streaming sources.

pitfalls.title: Expecting readStream to start processing
pitfalls.text: readStream only defines a plan; nothing runs until a sink is started.
pitfalls.fix: Start the query with `writeStream ... toTable()/start()`.

pitfalls.title: Trigger interval ≠ completion guarantee
pitfalls.text: A 5-second trigger with 12-second batches builds a backlog; batches don't run in parallel.
pitfalls.fix: Treat sustained overrun as capacity problem; fix capacity/query/skew.

pitfalls.title: Using Trigger.Once
pitfalls.text: Once is deprecated.
pitfalls.fix: Use `trigger(availableNow=True)`.

pitfalls.title: processingTime on serverless
pitfalls.text: Serverless notebooks/jobs don't support time-based or real-time triggers.
pitfalls.fix: Use AvailableNow on a schedule, or a Lakeflow pipeline in continuous mode for always-on.

pitfalls.title: Real-time mode for ordinary ETL
pitfalls.text: Ultra-low latency adds cost/complexity most lakehouse ETL doesn't need.
pitfalls.fix: Default to micro-batch or AvailableNow.

pitfalls.title: Unbounded state
pitfalls.text: Stateful queries without a time bound (aggregation, dedup, joins) keep keys forever → memory, checkpoint size, slow batches, OOM.
pitfalls.fix: Add watermarks, window/time bounds, dedup horizon; review key cardinality.

pitfalls.title: Arrival time ≠ event time
pitfalls.text: Windowing or watermarking on processing/ingest time puts late events in the wrong window or drops them.
pitfalls.fix: Window and watermark on the event-time column.

pitfalls.title: Watermark as a wall-clock timer
pitfalls.text: Lateness is relative to max observed event time, not to now − event_time.
pitfalls.fix: Reason: watermark ≈ max event time − delay.

pitfalls.title: Watermark too short
pitfalls.text: Valid late records beyond the tolerance may be dropped.
pitfalls.fix: Size it from measured real lateness; accept the state/latency cost.

pitfalls.title: Watermark as retention policy
pitfalls.text: A watermark never deletes table rows; it only affects streaming state and late data.
pitfalls.fix: Use DELETE/retention/VACUUM for data lifecycle.

pitfalls.title: Watermark after the aggregation
pitfalls.text: Defined after groupBy, it can't bound the aggregation's state.
pitfalls.fix: Call withWatermark before groupBy, on the window's time column.

pitfalls.title: Update mode into a Delta sink
pitfalls.text: The Delta sink supports append and complete only.
pitfalls.fix: Use foreachBatch + MERGE for update-like results.

pitfalls.title: Complete mode on high-cardinality aggregates
pitfalls.text: Complete mode doesn't evict state via watermark and rewrites everything.
pitfalls.fix: Prefer append/update with watermark, or MERGE.

pitfalls.title: Append output 'delayed'
pitfalls.text: Append emits windows only once final (window end + watermark).
pitfalls.fix: Explain expected delay or provide a live MERGE table.

pitfalls.title: Deleting or changing the checkpoint
pitfalls.text: The query restarts as new: reprocessing, duplicate side effects, lost state.
pitfalls.fix: Keep one stable checkpoint per query; resets only deliberately (sandbox / planned backfill).

pitfalls.title: Assuming new code reuses the checkpoint
pitfalls.text: Changing state keys/schema/source/stateful operators can be checkpoint-incompatible.
pitfalls.fix: Check compatibility rules and test stateful deployments.

pitfalls.title: Exactly-once ≠ no duplicates
pitfalls.text: Source duplicates pass through; non-idempotent foreachBatch side effects replay.
pitfalls.fix: Dedup business keys; make side effects idempotent.

pitfalls.title: Non-idempotent foreachBatch
pitfalls.text: Retries can call the function twice (balance += x, emails).
pitfalls.fix: MERGE by business key/version or transactional sink semantics.

pitfalls.title: Unbounded dropDuplicates
pitfalls.text: dropDuplicates without a watermark remembers every key forever.
pitfalls.fix: Watermark + include event_time, or dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark.

pitfalls.title: Stream-stream join without watermarks
pitfalls.text: Join state grows without bound; outer joins are rejected.
pitfalls.fix: Watermarks on both inputs + time-range join condition.

pitfalls.title: Using max multiple-watermark policy casually
pitfalls.text: Faster progress but records of the slower stream may be dropped.
pitfalls.fix: Keep the default min unless you accept the loss.

pitfalls.title: Expecting stream-static joins to recompute history
pitfalls.text: A changed dimension doesn't rewrite already-written outputs.
pitfalls.fix: Use materialized/declarative patterns if recomputation is required.

pitfalls.title: Stopping a Delta-source stream longer than retention
pitfalls.text: Vacuumed files make incremental catch-up impossible.
pitfalls.fix: Run at least once per retention window; increase retention.

pitfalls.title: ignoreMissingFiles as a fix
pitfalls.text: Hides missing data → silent incorrect results.
pitfalls.fix: Increase retention or recover/rebuild the stream.

pitfalls.title: UPDATE/DELETE on a Delta streaming source
pitfalls.text: A plain Delta source is append-oriented; change commits break or get skipped.
pitfalls.fix: Use Change Data Feed or skipChangeCommits deliberately.

pitfalls.title: Tiny triggers → small files
pitfalls.text: Every micro-batch writes small files and commits.
pitfalls.fix: Choose a sensible latency; rely on OPTIMIZE/predictive optimization.

pitfalls.title: Thinking a checkpoint adds throughput
pitfalls.text: Checkpoint preserves progress; it doesn't create capacity.
pitfalls.fix: Add capacity, cheaper query, less state, less skew.

pitfalls.title: Skewed stateful key
pitfalls.text: One hot key (e.g. 'anonymous') creates a hot state partition that slows every batch.
pitfalls.fix: Redesign keys / handle hot keys separately.

pitfalls.title: Checkpoint = 'last timestamp'
pitfalls.text: A checkpoint stores offsets, commits, state and query metadata — not just a timestamp.
pitfalls.fix: Treat it as the query's identity and durable memory.

pitfalls.title: AvailableNow = run forever
pitfalls.text: AvailableNow processes the currently available backlog incrementally and then stops.
pitfalls.fix: Schedule it (e.g. hourly) for incremental batch; use continuous modes for always-on.

pitfalls.title: Restarting blindly
pitfalls.text: Restarts (especially with new checkpoints) destroy evidence and can duplicate data.
pitfalls.fix: Inspect status/lastProgress first.
