exercises.q: Test Q1: Why can Spark Structured Streaming reuse batch-like DataFrame syntax?
options: Because it converts streams into files first and runs a nightly batch
Because it uses Spark's DataFrame/query-planning execution model incrementally over unbounded input
Because streaming DataFrames are just pandas DataFrames refreshed every second
Because it only supports SQL, and SQL is the same everywhere
why: No — it processes incrementally as data becomes available, not as a nightly batch.
Correct — same planner and engine, incremental execution.
No — Spark DataFrames are distributed; pandas has nothing to do with it.
No — the DataFrame API (Python) is reused, not only SQL.
exercises.explain: Structured Streaming is the same Spark engine: the same planner turns your DataFrame code into jobs, applied **incrementally** to new data. It does not secretly batch files nightly, and it is not pandas.

exercises.q: Structured Streaming is a separate execution engine from batch Spark, with its own notion of jobs and tasks.
exercises.explain: It is the **same** Spark execution engine. A micro-batch is a normal Spark job with stages, tasks and partitions; only the input is treated as unbounded and processed incrementally.

exercises.q: Bounded or unbounded input?

items.text: JSON files landing in a Volume forever
Rows appended continuously to a Bronze Delta table
A fixed reference CSV of country codes

exercises.explain: Bounded = known end, process once and stop. Unbounded = logically keeps growing, the query must keep (or repeatedly) process new data.

exercises.q: Put the Phase 5 mental model in order (top to bottom).
exercises.explain: Source → readStream defines it → a plan is built → the trigger decides when → micro-batch executes → operators (stateless/stateful) → writeStream → sink, with the checkpoint remembering progress + state alongside.

exercises.q: Complete the unbounded-table idea.
exercises.text: Structured Streaming treats a stream as a table that keeps [[growing|growing forever]]: each new event is a new [[row]]. The engine runs your query [[incrementally]] over the new rows while the [[checkpoint]] remembers progress and state.
exercises.explain: The unbounded-table model is the core of Structured Streaming: same query, incremental execution, checkpointed progress.

exercises.q: Which item does NOT belong to the streaming mental model chain?
exercises.explain: readStream, trigger and checkpoint are all parts of a streaming query. **VACUUM** is Delta table file garbage collection — a storage maintenance command, not part of the streaming pipeline (though it can break a stopped stream, section 12).

exercises.q: Explain in 3–4 sentences the difference between a bounded and an unbounded dataset, and why the second needs a checkpoint.
exercises.model: A bounded dataset has a known end: you read it all, compute and stop. An unbounded dataset logically never ends — new records keep arriving — so the query keeps running or re-running on new data. Because it runs over and over, the engine must durably remember which input it already processed (and any intermediate state), otherwise a restart would reprocess or skip data. That memory is the checkpoint.
rubric: checkpoint remembers progress (and state) across restarts
exercises.explain: This is the first-principles core: unboundedness is what forces progress tracking.

exercises.q: Test Q3: `spark.readStream...load(path)` immediately starts processing files.
exercises.explain: No. readStream only defines a streaming source / logical plan (lazy evaluation). Execution starts when a streaming sink is started with `writeStream ... toTable()` or `.start()`.

exercises.q: Certification trap: what is the difference between `spark.read` and `spark.readStream`?
options: None — readStream is just a faster read
read = bounded batch read; readStream = streaming source tracked incrementally
read works only on Delta; readStream only on Kafka
readStream reads the whole table every second
why: They have different execution models, not different speeds.
Correct.
Both work with many formats (json, Delta, etc.).
No — it processes only new data incrementally.
exercises.explain: `spark.read` reads what exists now (bounded). `spark.readStream` treats the source as continuously evolving and tracks progress. Simple but frequently tested.

exercises.q: This cell fails with an error about `writeStream`. Which line is the bug?
exercises.explain: `spark.read` creates a **batch** DataFrame; `.writeStream` can only be called on a streaming DataFrame. Use `spark.readStream`.

exercises.q: Fill in the streaming read.
exercises.explain: Streaming file sources take an explicit `.schema(...)` — then `.load(path)` builds the streaming DataFrame (still lazy).

exercises.q: Complete the sink that STARTS the query.
exercises.explain: `writeStream` defines the sink, `checkpointLocation` gives the query its durable memory, `toTable(...)` starts the query writing to a table.

exercises.q: Match each piece to its role.
exercises.explain: Only the start call triggers execution; everything before it is plan-building.

exercises.q: Write a stream that reads the Delta table `ecommerce.bronze.events`, keeps rows where `event_type IS NOT NULL`, and writes to `ecommerce.silver.events` with checkpoint variable `checkpoint`.
exercises.solution:
events = spark.readStream.table("ecommerce.bronze.events")
clean = events.filter("event_type IS NOT NULL")
query = (
    clean.writeStream
        .option("checkpointLocation", checkpoint)
        .toTable("ecommerce.silver.events")
)
exercises.explain: Source → transformation → sink. Delta-to-Delta streaming needs only `readStream.table`, a transformation and `writeStream...toTable` with a checkpoint.

exercises.q: Which StreamingQuery call blocks until the query stops — typical at the end of a job script?
exercises.explain: `awaitTermination()` blocks; `status` and `lastProgress`/`recentProgress` only report what's happening.

exercises.q: In production, a `writeStream` to a table should always set a durable `checkpointLocation`.
exercises.explain: Without a durable checkpoint the query can't remember offsets, commits and state across restarts — it would behave as a new query each time.

exercises.q: Test Q2: What is a micro-batch?
options: A single event processed by its own Spark job
A bounded chunk of newly available stream data executed as a Spark job
A small cluster dedicated to streaming
A Delta file smaller than 128 MB
why: That's the misconception micro-batching avoids.
Correct.
It's a unit of work, not compute.
Unrelated to file sizes.
exercises.explain: Micro-batch = bounded chunk of new data → one Spark job (stages, tasks, partitions). Spark does not launch a job per event.

exercises.q: Inside a micro-batch, concepts like shuffle, skew, spill and partitions no longer apply because streaming has its own engine.
exercises.explain: Each micro-batch is a normal Spark job: job → stages → tasks → partitions. Shuffle, joins, spill and skew all still apply (Chapter 9).

exercises.q: Trigger = every 5 seconds, but each micro-batch needs 12 seconds. Batches run sequentially. How many micro-batches COMPLETE in the first 60 seconds?
exercises.explain: Batches don't overlap: they finish at 12, 24, 36, 48, 60 s → **5** batches. Twelve were 'scheduled' by the 5-s trigger, so a backlog builds and latency grows.

exercises.q: Trigger every 5 s, a micro-batch takes 12 s. What does Spark do in the normal micro-batch model?
options: Runs 3 batches in parallel to catch up
Skips the data of the missed triggers
Starts the next batch after the current one finishes; backlog and latency grow
Fails the query with a trigger timeout
exercises.explain: Micro-batches are sequential. No data is skipped and no parallel batches run — the query just falls behind: processing backlog + growing latency.

exercises.q: Complete the 5-second trigger.
exercises.explain: `processingTime` sets how often Spark tries to start a new micro-batch.

exercises.q: A processingTime trigger of 5 seconds guarantees every micro-batch completes within 5 seconds.
exercises.explain: It only schedules **attempts**. If a batch takes longer, the next one starts late — the trigger can't create capacity.

exercises.q: Arrange the execution hierarchy of one micro-batch.
exercises.explain: Each micro-batch becomes a Spark job, split into stages, executed by tasks — one task per partition.

exercises.q: Batches consistently take longer than the trigger interval. What is this production signal?
options: The sink is in update mode
exercises.explain: Sustained overrun = the pipeline can't process data as fast as it arrives. Fix with capacity, a cheaper query, less state or less skew — not with the trigger.

exercises.q: Test Q4: What is AvailableNow?
options: Run continuously with the lowest latency
Process all currently available unprocessed input incrementally, then stop
Reprocess the entire source from the beginning, then stop
Process exactly one row, then stop
why: That's processingTime/real-time, not AvailableNow.
Correct.
No — only unprocessed input; the checkpoint remembers the rest.
No such semantics.
exercises.explain: AvailableNow = catch up on everything available now (possibly in several batches), then stop. The checkpoint makes the next run start where this one ended.

exercises.q: Test Q5: Why is AvailableNow useful for Data Engineering?
exercises.model: Scheduled incremental jobs get checkpointed streaming semantics — incremental source tracking, checkpointing, state management, fault recovery — without an always-on process. You schedule it (e.g. hourly), it processes everything new since the last run and stops, so you pay only while it runs and never hand-write last_processed_timestamp logic.
exercises.explain: This is why Databricks recommends AvailableNow especially on serverless jobs, and why Auto Loader jobs commonly use it.

exercises.q: Match the trigger to its behaviour.
pairs: next micro-batch as soon as the previous finishes
process the available backlog, then stop
sub-second operational latency on supported classic
exercises.explain: Default = processingTime 0. Once was deprecated in favour of AvailableNow.

exercises.q: Databricks recommends `Trigger.Once` over `Trigger.AvailableNow` for new scheduled jobs.
exercises.explain: Reverse: Once is **deprecated** in favour of AvailableNow, which can split a large backlog into multiple batches and still stops at the end.

exercises.q: On serverless notebooks/jobs, is this trigger supported?
exercises.explain: Serverless: AvailableNow ✅, Once ✅ (deprecated), ProcessingTime ❌, RealTime ❌. Always-on serverless streaming → Lakeflow pipeline continuous mode.

exercises.q: Certification trap: you need an ALWAYS-RUNNING stream on serverless. What's the preferred architecture?
options: Serverless job with .trigger(availableNow=True) in a while-true loop
A Lakeflow pipeline in continuous mode
Real-time mode on a serverless SQL warehouse
why: processingTime isn't supported on serverless notebooks/jobs.
A hack; AvailableNow is meant for scheduled runs.
Correct.
Real-time mode is for supported classic environments, not SQL warehouses.
exercises.explain: Time-based triggers aren't supported on serverless notebooks/jobs, and real-time mode is classic-only. For continuously running serverless workloads Databricks directs you to Lakeflow pipelines' continuous mode (Phase 6).

exercises.q: Write the hourly incremental job: trigger that processes what's available then stops, checkpoint `checkpoint`, target `ecommerce.bronze.events`.
exercises.explain: Schedule this hourly: run 1 processes A B C, run 2 processes only D E because the checkpoint remembers A B C.

exercises.q: An hourly AvailableNow job ran at 10:00 and processed files A, B, C. At 11:00 it runs again; only D and E are new.

steps.prompt: What does the 11:00 run process?

options.text: Only D and E, then stops
options.fb: Right — the checkpoint knows A B C were processed.

options.text: A, B, C, D, E again
options.fb: Only if the checkpoint were deleted or changed.

options.text: Nothing until a new trigger interval passes
options.fb: AvailableNow doesn't wait for intervals; it processes the available backlog.

steps.prompt: At 12:00 nothing new has arrived. What happens?

options.text: It finds no new offsets and stops quickly
options.fb: Correct — nothing new to process.

options.text: It waits forever for new data
options.fb: That's the default/processingTime behaviour, not AvailableNow.

options.text: It fails because there is no data
options.fb: An empty backlog is a normal outcome.

exercises.explain: AvailableNow + checkpoint = incremental batch semantics without hand-written progress tracking.

exercises.q: Which is NOT something AvailableNow gives you for free compared with a hand-written `WHERE event_ts > last_ts` job?
exercises.explain: The streaming engine tracks progress, recovers and manages state. It does **not** deduplicate business duplicates — that remains your job.

exercises.q: Real-time mode should be the default choice for ordinary lakehouse ETL because lower latency is always better.
exercises.explain: Real-time mode targets ultra-low-latency operational workloads. For normal lakehouse ETL, micro-batch or AvailableNow is simpler, cheaper and easier to operate.

exercises.q: Test Q6: Stateless vs stateful?
options: Stateless never writes to a sink; stateful does
Stateless processing doesn't need historical intermediate state; stateful does
Stateless uses Python; stateful uses SQL
Stateless runs on serverless; stateful only on classic
exercises.explain: Stateless keeps only progress tracking; stateful keeps intermediate state (counts, open windows, join buffers, dedup keys) across micro-batches.

exercises.q: Test Q7: In a streaming query, `groupBy(...).count()` is stateful.
exercises.explain: Q8 — why: the aggregate result must accumulate information across micro-batches (customer 42: 5, then 8), so Spark keeps state.

exercises.q: Stateless or stateful in Structured Streaming?
exercises.explain: Aggregations, distinct/dropDuplicates, stream-stream joins and custom stateful operations keep state. A stream-static join doesn't buffer the stream side.

exercises.q: Test Q8: Why is a streaming groupBy stateful? Use the customer-42 example.
exercises.model: Because the result must accumulate across micro-batches. If batch 1 had 5 events for customer 42 and batch 2 brings 3 more, Spark can only output 8 if it remembered the 5 from batch 1. That remembered running count is state, kept in the distributed state store and checkpointed.
exercises.explain: State = information from previous micro-batches needed to process the next ones correctly.

exercises.q: `groupBy("customer_id").count()` with no watermark; 1 million NEW customers appear every day and none is ever forgotten. How many million keys are in state after 30 days?
exercises.explain: 1M × 30 days = **30M** keys (365M after a year). State grows forever → more memory, bigger checkpoints, slower lookups, slower batches, potential OOM.

exercises.q: Unbounded state: order the consequences as they snowball.
exercises.explain: Growing state first costs memory and checkpoint size, then slows every lookup and batch, and finally can OOM.

exercises.q: Test Q34: Which state-store technology does Databricks currently recommend for demanding stateful workloads?
options: A Delta table rewritten every batch
why: State is distributed, not a driver dict.
Correct.
Not how state is stored.
Photon is an execution engine, not a state store.
exercises.explain: RocksDB state store + changelog checkpointing scales state and reduces state-checkpoint overhead/latency. State is distributed across executors — never a driver dict.

exercises.q: When state becomes the bottleneck, scaling up compute is always the right fix.
exercises.explain: Not necessarily. The state design (watermark, key cardinality, join bounds) and the state-store architecture (RocksDB + changelog checkpointing) may matter more than node size.

exercises.q: Complete the definition.
exercises.text: State is information from previous [[micro-batches|batches]] that is needed to correctly process the [[next|following]] ones. It is the [[working memory]] of the computation, not the final output.
exercises.explain: That's why state must be checkpointed — losing it means wrong (restarted-from-zero) aggregates.

exercises.q: Three of these are stateful operators. Which one is the odd one out?
exercises.explain: A projection with a computed column is stateless: each row is handled alone.

exercises.q: The state of `groupBy("session_id").count()` grows by millions of rows every day and batches keep slowing down. There is no watermark.

steps.prompt: Why is state growing forever?

options.text: New session_ids keep appearing and nothing tells Spark it can forget old ones
options.fb: Unbounded key cardinality with no time bound.

options.text: The checkpoint is duplicated
options.fb: No evidence of that.

options.text: Append mode stores every row twice
options.fb: Not how output modes work.

steps.prompt: What is the most effective fix?

options.text: Add an event-time window + watermark so old sessions' state can be evicted
options.fb: Bound the state semantically.

options.text: Double the cluster
options.fb: Buys time; state keeps growing.

options.text: Use complete mode
options.fb: Complete mode never evicts state.

exercises.explain: State store huge: maybe the state is semantically unbounded — fix the semantics before the hardware.

exercises.q: State store huge: order the checks (Keys, Clock, Joins, Dedup, Skew).
exercises.explain: Each item is a reason state can't be evicted or is concentrated.

exercises.q: Test Q9: What is event time?
options: When the event occurred, according to the event data
When the file was written to storage
exercises.explain: Event time is a column carried by the data (event_time). Processing time (Q10) is when the engine observes/processes the record.

exercises.q: Test Q10 & certification trap: match each time concept.
pairs: how often a micro-batch is attempted
exercises.explain: Watermarks are based on **event time**, triggers on **processing time** (wall clock).

exercises.q: Test Q11: which of these can make event time EARLIER than processing time?

items.text: batch upload of a day's events

exercises.explain: Network delays, offline clients, queues/backlogs, outages, retries, batch uploads and clock skew all delay arrival. Output mode and sink type don't change when the event happened.

exercises.q: 10-minute tumbling windows. An event has event_time 10:03 and arrives at 10:11. Which window START does it belong to? (answer as HHMM, e.g. 1000)
exercises.explain: Windows are assigned by **event time**: 10:03 → [10:00–10:10), start 10:00. Arrival at 10:11 is irrelevant to the window choice.

exercises.q: 5-minute tumbling windows. Event_time 10:47:30. Window START? (HHMM)
Sliding window: `F.window("event_time", "1 hour", "15 minutes")`. In how many windows does each event land?
exercises.explain: Overlapping windows: window ÷ slide = 60 ÷ 15 = **4**. A tumbling window (no slide) puts each event in exactly 1.

exercises.q: Write the revenue-per-10-minute-window aggregation.
exercises.text:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
sales = (
    events
        .groupBy(F.[[window]]("[[event_time]]", "10 minutes"))
        .agg(F.[[sum]]("amount").alias("revenue"))
)
exercises.explain: `F.window(timeCol, duration)` creates tumbling event-time windows; group by it and aggregate.

exercises.q: A purchase at event_time 10:03 that arrives at 10:11 is counted in the 10:10–10:20 window because that's when Spark saw it.
exercises.explain: Event-time windows use event time: it belongs to 10:00–10:10. Using arrival time would put revenue in the wrong period.

exercises.q: Late data trade-off: what happens if you keep every window open forever?
options: Low state but lost late data
Correct for arbitrarily late data but infinite state
exercises.explain: Waiting forever = correct but unbounded state. Closing immediately = low state but lost late data. The watermark is the compromise.

exercises.q: Test Q12: What does a watermark solve?
options: It deletes old rows from the Delta table
It bounds state and sets a threshold for late-data handling/finalization
why: That's VACUUM/retention territory, not watermarks.
Correct.
Triggers are separate.
Dedup is a separate stateful op.
exercises.explain: Watermark = bound state + tolerated lateness/finalization. It is not a retention policy and doesn't touch table rows.

exercises.q: Test Q13: `withWatermark("event_time", "10 minutes")` means each event is accepted for exactly 10 wall-clock minutes after it was created.
exercises.explain: No. The watermark is relative to the **maximum observed event time** (watermark ≈ max event time − 10 min), not to each row's wall-clock age.

exercises.q: Max event time seen so far = 12:00, watermark delay 10 minutes. Conceptual watermark? (HHMM)
exercises.explain: watermark ≈ max event time − delay = 12:00 − 10 min = **11:50**. State older than that may be finalized/evicted.

exercises.q: Max event time seen = 10:20, delay = 5 min. An event with event_time 10:03 arrives now. What happens?
options: Accepted — it arrived within 20 wall-clock minutes
It is older than the watermark (≈10:15) → too late, may be dropped
It's assigned to the current window instead
exercises.explain: Watermark ≈ 10:20 − 5 = 10:15. 10:03 is behind it → too late. With a 30-min delay (watermark ≈ 09:50) it would still be accepted.

exercises.q: Lab 7 variant: max event time seen = 10:20, watermark delay 30 minutes. What is the conceptual watermark? (HHMM)
exercises.explain: 10:20 − 30 min = **09:50**. An event at 10:03 is newer than that → accepted and still updates its window's state.

exercises.q: Short (5 min) or long (2 h) watermark?

items.text: late records beyond tolerance may be dropped

exercises.explain: Test Q14/Q15: short = less state and lower latency, but lower tolerance for late data. Long = more tolerance, more state, memory, checkpoint size and latency.

exercises.q: Certification trap: a 7-day watermark on a streaming table makes Databricks delete table rows older than 7 days.
exercises.explain: A watermark only affects streaming **state** and late-data handling. Historical rows stay; deletion is DELETE/retention/VACUUM territory.

exercises.q: Late is relative to query progress: an event that arrives 20 minutes after it happened can still be accepted with a 10-minute watermark.
exercises.explain: If the max event time seen is only, say, 5 minutes ahead of it, the watermark is still behind its event time → accepted. Lateness ≠ now − event_time.

exercises.q: Add a 15-minute watermark on `event_time`, then sum `amount` as `revenue` per 10-minute window and `country`.
exercises.solution:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
sales = (
    events
        .withWatermark("event_time", "15 minutes")
        .groupBy(F.window("event_time", "10 minutes"), F.col("country"))
        .agg(F.sum("amount").alias("revenue"))
)
exercises.explain: Watermark first (on the same event-time column used by the window), then the windowed aggregation — so old window state can be evicted.

exercises.q: This aggregation keeps growing state and the watermark never cleans anything. Which line is wrong?
exercises.explain: The watermark must be defined **before** the aggregation, on the event-time column the window uses. Applied afterwards, it can't bound the aggregation's state (and append mode on the aggregate isn't allowed).

exercises.q: Late events are dropped although they are only minutes late in business terms. Spot the semantic bug.
exercises.explain: The watermark is on processing/ingest time, not on the event-time column used by the window. Watermarks must use **event time** — the timestamp that represents reality.

exercises.q: Interview: 'A watermark is just a timer per row.' Correct this statement.
exercises.model: A watermark is an event-time progress threshold, not a per-row timer. Spark tracks the maximum event time it has observed and sets watermark ≈ max event time − delay; the actual value is guaranteed to lag at least by the delay but isn't an exact instantaneous cutoff (it's coordinated across partitions and updated between micro-batches). Events older than the watermark may be dropped and state for windows behind it can be finalized and evicted.
rubric: not exact / at least delay behind
lets state be evicted and late data be handled
exercises.explain: Being precise here signals you understand why 'late' depends on query progress.

exercises.q: Lab 7: you send event_time 10:01 (arrives 10:01), 10:02 (arrives 10:02) and 10:03 (arrives 10:20) with a 5-minute watermark. The 10:03 event is still counted. A teammate says 'the watermark is broken'.

steps.prompt: What is the max event time seen when the 10:03 event arrives?

options.fb: Right — only event times count, and the latest was 10:02.
That's the arrival (processing) time, not event time.
10:03 is the late event itself; before it, the max was 10:02.

steps.prompt: So is the 10:03 event late in event-time terms?

options.text: No — watermark ≈ 09:57, the event is ahead of it
options.fb: Correct: lateness is relative to event-time progress.

options.text: Yes, it's 18 minutes late so it must be dropped
options.fb: Wall-clock delay doesn't define lateness.

options.text: It depends on the trigger interval
options.fb: Triggers don't define lateness.

steps.prompt: How do you make the lab show the difference between 5- and 30-minute watermarks?

options.text: First send an on-time event with event_time ≈ 10:20, let a batch pass, then send the 10:03 event
options.fb: Now 5 min → watermark ≈ 10:15 (dropped) vs 30 min → ≈ 09:50 (accepted).

options.text: Delete the checkpoint between runs
options.fb: Irrelevant to lateness and dangerous habit.

options.text: Switch to complete mode
options.fb: Complete mode doesn't evict state; it hides the effect.

exercises.explain: Watermarks are event-time based: you must advance event time to make an event 'late'.

exercises.q: Missing late records: order the event-time chain (E-M-W-P-O-W).
items: max observed event time at arrival
exercises.explain: Reason in event time. Only blame the checkpoint if evidence points there.

exercises.q: Test Q22, Q23, Q24: match the output mode.
pairs: emits changed aggregate rows each trigger
emits the complete aggregate result each trigger
exercises.explain: Append = finalized, Update = changed, Complete = everything.

exercises.q: Test Q25: The Delta streaming sink supports update output mode directly.
exercises.explain: No. Delta sinks support append and complete. Update-like semantics into Delta are implemented with foreachBatch + MERGE.

exercises.q: Batch 1: GR 100, DE 50. Batch 2 adds +50 for GR and a new FR 20. What does COMPLETE mode emit after batch 2?
exercises.explain: Complete re-emits the whole result every trigger. Update would emit GR 150 and FR 20 (the changed rows). Append would wait for finality.

exercises.q: Same data: what does UPDATE mode emit after batch 2?
exercises.explain: Update emits only rows whose result changed in this trigger: GR (100→150) and the new FR. DE didn't change.

exercises.q: This query fails at start. Which line is the problem?
exercises.fix:
(counts.writeStream
    .outputMode("append")      # or foreachBatch + MERGE for live updates
    .option("checkpointLocation", ckpt)
    .toTable("ecommerce.gold.event_counts"))
exercises.explain: The Delta table sink doesn't support update mode. Use append (finalized windows) or foreachBatch + MERGE for update-like behaviour.

exercises.q: This aggregation is rejected in append mode. Why?
exercises.explain: Append emits only final rows; without a watermark no aggregate can ever be final, so Spark refuses append for streaming aggregations without a watermark. Add `withWatermark` on the event-time column before the groupBy.

exercises.q: In complete mode, the watermark evicts old aggregation state just like in append/update mode.
exercises.explain: Complete mode must re-emit the whole result, so aggregation state is **not** evicted by the watermark — expensive with large/unbounded cardinality.

exercises.q: For a stateless filter/select stream, choosing append vs update makes no real semantic difference.
exercises.explain: No row ever changes later, so the output-mode distinction doesn't change operator behaviour (complete isn't allowed without an aggregation).

exercises.q: Event analytics example: 5-minute windows, 20-minute watermark, append mode. Roughly what max event time must the stream observe before window [10:00–10:05) is emitted? (HHMM)
exercises.explain: The window is final when the watermark (max event time − 20 min) reaches its end 10:05 → max event time ≈ **10:25** (and the next micro-batch runs). That's why append output looks 'delayed'.

exercises.q: A product manager complains: 'Events arrive instantly in Bronze, but ecommerce.gold.event_counts (5-min windows, 20-min watermark, append) shows nothing for the last half hour. The stream is lagging!'

steps.prompt: What do you check first?

options.text: Compare the latest event times with the current watermark in query.lastProgress
options.fb: Right — append only emits windows the watermark has passed.

options.text: Restart the cluster
options.fb: Restarting blindly hides evidence and doesn't change semantics.

options.text: Delete the checkpoint to 'reset' the stream
options.fb: Dangerous: reprocessing and duplicates.

steps.prompt: Watermark is 20 min behind the max event time; batches are fast. Diagnosis?

options.text: Intended behaviour: windows are emitted once final
options.fb: Correct — stateful aggregate + append + watermark = wait for finality.

options.text: Backlog: input rate > processing rate
options.fb: Batches are fast; rates would show it.

options.text: Corrupted state store
options.fb: No evidence points there.

steps.prompt: The PM really needs live-updating counts. What do you propose?

options.text: foreachBatch + MERGE into a live counts table (update-like semantics)
options.fb: Yes — Delta sink doesn't support update mode directly.

options.text: Switch the Delta sink to outputMode("update")
options.fb: Delta sinks don't support update mode.

options.text: Set the watermark to 0 seconds
options.fb: That drops valid late data and still isn't 'live update'.

exercises.explain: Append output looking delayed is often intended. Live dashboards need update-like semantics via foreachBatch + MERGE.

exercises.q: Write the Gold writer for the event-analytics `counts` DataFrame: append mode, checkpoint `/Volumes/ecommerce/system/event_counts_ckpt`, table `ecommerce.gold.event_counts`.
exercises.explain: Append + watermark gives one final row per window and event_type, and lets window state be removed afterwards.

exercises.q: Order the lifecycle of one window in the event-analytics example.
items: Spark keeps counts in state per event_type
a late event (10:04) updates the window state
the watermark advances past the window end
append mode emits the final row once
exercises.explain: That's the complete lifecycle: accumulate, absorb late data, finalize at the watermark, emit once, evict state.

exercises.q: Test Q16: What does a streaming checkpoint contain?
options: Offsets/progress, commit information, query metadata and state where applicable
A full copy of the sink table
why: The classic trap answer.
Correct.
The sink data lives in the sink.
Code isn't stored in the checkpoint.
exercises.explain: offsets/ (what each batch reads), commits/ (what was written), state/ (stateful operators) and metadata (query identity). Certification trap: it's not just a 'last timestamp'.

exercises.q: Test Q17: What happens if the checkpoint is deleted (or the checkpointLocation changed)?
options: The stream resumes exactly where it stopped
The query starts as new and loses prior progress/state identity
Databricks rebuilds it from the Delta log automatically
Only the state is lost; offsets are kept in the sink
exercises.explain: Deleting/changing the checkpoint = a new query: reprocessing, duplicate external side effects, lost accumulated state, maybe a full rebuild.

exercises.q: Match each checkpoint folder to what it records.
pairs: micro-batches successfully written to the sink
exercises.explain: Offsets are written before a batch runs, commits after the sink succeeds — that pair lets a restart decide skip vs retry.

exercises.q: Deploying new code on the SAME checkpoint: usually OK or dangerous?

items.text: renaming a projected column in a stateless query
switching the source from Kafka to Delta

exercises.explain: Some stateless changes can reuse a checkpoint depending on the exact query. State keys, state schema, source type and the number/type of stateful operators are checkpoint-incompatible changes.

exercises.q: A checkpoint folder is a generic progress folder that two different streaming queries can safely share.
exercises.explain: A checkpoint encodes one query's identity, offsets, commits and state. Sharing it between queries corrupts progress semantics. One checkpoint ↔ one query.

exercises.q: Why is 'state schema effectively production data'?
exercises.model: Because a stateful query's checkpoint holds state with a specific schema (keys and values). If you change the state architecture, the old checkpoint becomes incompatible and you may need a new checkpoint plus a full recomputation/backfill — which is expensive. So changing state keys or aggregations must be planned and tested like a data migration.
rubric: state lives in the checkpoint with a schema
exercises.explain: Stateless changes are cheap; stateful changes can cost a full rebuild.

exercises.q: You deploy a new version of a stateful query: groupBy changed from customer_id to country. You restart it on the existing checkpoint and it fails at start.

steps.prompt: What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The new state schema is incompatible with the checkpoint's state
options.fb: Right — state keys changed.

options.text: The cluster is too small
options.fb: It fails before processing any data.

options.text: The source is out of retention
options.fb: Possible in general, but the change you just made is the obvious suspect.

steps.prompt: What is the correct way forward?

options.text: New checkpoint + plan a full recomputation/backfill of the result
options.fb: Yes — and do it deliberately, ideally tested in non-prod first.

options.text: Delete files inside state/ until it starts
options.fb: Hand-editing a checkpoint corrupts query identity.

options.text: Point the old checkpoint at a different table
options.fb: Doesn't fix the state incompatibility.

exercises.explain: Stateful changes can be checkpoint-incompatible; the way out is a new checkpoint + backfill.

exercises.q: Write-ahead sequence of one micro-batch (why restarts are safe).
items: record the planned source range in offsets/
commit the result to the Delta sink
exercises.explain: Offsets first (plan), then process, then the sink commit, then the commit log. On restart, an offsets entry without a commit entry tells Spark which batch to check/redo.

exercises.q: Fill in the checkpoint-reset consequences.
exercises.text: Deleting a checkpoint can mean [[reprocessing]], duplicate external [[side effects]], loss of accumulated [[state]], and a full [[rebuild|backfill]].
exercises.explain: Per pipeline the impact differs — but never treat a checkpoint reset as harmless.

exercises.q: Test Q18: An exactly-once Delta sink means the source cannot contain duplicates.
exercises.explain: Q19 — why not: processing guarantees don't deduplicate semantically duplicated input records. Two records with event_id=123 are two records.

exercises.q: Which three pieces cooperate so a retried micro-batch never becomes a partial/duplicate commit in a Delta sink?
options: source offsets + checkpoint commits + Delta transaction log
exercises.explain: Replayable source offsets, the checkpoint commit log and Delta's transactional log together give exactly-once into a Delta sink.

exercises.q: Micro-batch 20 reads events 1000–1100 and writes to a Delta sink. The driver crashes right at the boundary.

steps.prompt: On restart, what question must the engine answer first?

options.text: Was batch 20 committed?
options.fb: Exactly — offsets/20 exists; is there a commit?

options.text: Which events arrived during the crash?
options.fb: Not yet relevant; batch 20's range is already fixed in offsets/.

options.text: Should it switch to complete mode?
options.fb: Output mode isn't part of recovery.

steps.prompt: Batch 20 IS in the Delta log but commits/20 is missing. What happens?

options.text: It is not applied again
options.fb: Correct — Delta knows this query's batch 20 is committed.

options.text: It is appended a second time
options.fb: That's what exactly-once prevents for the Delta sink.

options.text: Half of it is re-applied
options.fb: Never 'half applied twice'.

steps.prompt: Batch 20 is NOT in the Delta log. What happens?

options.text: Batch 20 is retried with the same offsets 1000–1100
options.fb: Yes — same range, deterministic retry.

options.text: Events 1000–1100 are skipped
options.fb: That would lose data.

options.text: The stream starts from event 0
options.fb: Only a lost checkpoint does that.

exercises.explain: if committed → don't apply again; if not → retry. Never half applied twice.

exercises.q: Because Structured Streaming is exactly-once, a `foreachBatch` that sends emails sends each email exactly once even after a crash.
exercises.explain: Exactly-once stops at the boundaries. If the crash happens before the checkpoint commit, the batch replays and the emails are sent again. External services don't share Delta's transaction semantics.

exercises.q: A foreachBatch sends 100 emails per micro-batch. Batch 7 sends its 100 emails, then the process crashes before the checkpoint commit. After the retry succeeds, how many emails did batch 7's customers receive in total?
exercises.explain: The retry re-runs the function for the same batch → 100 + 100 = **200**. Make side effects idempotent (e.g. record sent ids keyed by business id/batch).

exercises.q: Deduplicate a stream on `event_id` with bounded state: 1-hour watermark on `event_time`.
exercises.explain: Including the watermarked event_time in the dedup keys lets Spark drop old keys as event time progresses. Without the watermark, every event_id is remembered forever.

exercises.q: This dedup stream ran fine for weeks; now batches slow down and memory keeps rising. Which line causes it?
exercises.explain: Without a time bound, dropDuplicates must remember every event_id ever seen → unbounded state. Add a watermark and include the event-time column.

exercises.q: Which statement does NOT belong with the others?
options: Unbounded dedup needs to remember every key forever
A watermark lets dedup state be cleaned
Exactly-once processing removes duplicate business events automatically
exercises.explain: The first three are true facts about streaming dedup. Exactly-once processing does NOT remove business duplicates — that's the trap.

exercises.q: You need to drop duplicates on `event_id` even when the duplicate copies carry slightly different `event_time` values, with bounded state. Which API fits best?
why: Unbounded state.
Correct (newer runtimes).
Bounded, but copies with different event_time aren't considered duplicates.
Unbounded and compares all columns.
exercises.explain: `dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark` dedups on the key alone within the watermark delay — copies with different timestamps still collapse. The classic `[event_id, event_time]` key treats different timestamps as different rows.

exercises.q: Duplicates after failure: order the questions.
items: Does the source itself contain duplicates?
exercises.explain: Sink type first (where exactly-once ends), then side effects, then source duplicates and checkpoint resets.

exercises.q: Test Q26: Why do stream-stream joins need state?
options: A record from one stream may need to wait for a later matching record from the other
Because the static side is cached in state
exercises.explain: An order at 10:00 must be kept until its payment (10:02) arrives. Q27: watermarks decide when that waiting state can be discarded.

exercises.q: Certification trap: for stream-stream OUTER joins, a watermark is required.
exercises.explain: The engine must know when an unmatched record can be considered final and emitted with NULLs — that's exactly what watermark + time constraint provide.

exercises.q: Orders watermark is at 13:50, payments watermark at 12:59. With the default multiple-watermark policy, what is the global watermark? (HHMM)
exercises.explain: Default policy = **min** → the slowest input decides: 12:59. With `max` it would be 13:50 and late payments could be dropped.

exercises.q: Why is 'min' the default multiple-watermark policy?
options: Global progress follows the slowest input, so state the slow stream still needs isn't discarded
exercises.explain: If orders are at 14:00 but payments only at 13:00, using the orders watermark could discard state while matching payments can still appear. min protects correctness; max trades correctness for progress.

exercises.q: Complete the stream-stream join setup.
exercises.text:
orders_w = orders.[[withWatermark]]("order_time", "30 minutes")
payments_w = payments.withWatermark("[[payment_time]]", "30 minutes")
joined = orders_w.alias("o").join(
    payments_w.alias("p"),
    F.expr("""o.order_id = p.order_id AND
              p.payment_time [[BETWEEN]] o.order_time AND o.order_time + INTERVAL 1 HOUR"""))
exercises.explain: Watermarks on both inputs + key + time-range condition let Spark discard obsolete join state.

exercises.q: This stream-stream left outer join is rejected. Which line is missing the essential piece?
lines: joined = orders_w.join(payments_s, F.expr("order_id = p_order_id AND payment_time BETWEEN order_time AND order_time + INTERVAL 1 HOUR"), "left_outer")
exercises.explain: Outer stream-stream joins require watermarks so unmatched rows can be finalized; Databricks recommends watermarks on BOTH inputs. The payments side has none.

exercises.q: In a long-running stream-static join, if the products dimension table is updated, Spark automatically recomputes all previously written enriched rows.
exercises.explain: Already-written outputs are not recomputed. New micro-batches may see the newer version, but history stays as it was. If correctness needs recomputation, consider materialized/declarative pipeline patterns (Phase 6).

exercises.q: Enrich `orders_stream` with the static table `ecommerce.silver.products` on `product_id`.
exercises.explain: Stream-static join: the static side is read with spark.table (batch). Very common for dimension enrichment.

exercises.q: Stream-static or stream-stream join?

items.text: static side may change without recomputing history
buffers records waiting for a future match

exercises.explain: Only stream-stream joins buffer both sides in state and need watermarks/time bounds.

exercises.q: Test Q28: Why can a stream fail if it was stopped beyond the Delta source's retention?
options: The checkpoint expires automatically after 7 days
Required source versions/files may have been vacuumed before the stream catches up
Delta tables can't be read by streams after 7 days
The watermark deletes the source rows
exercises.explain: The checkpoint says 'I need version X', but VACUUM removed the physical files. The stream can't recover incrementally.

exercises.q: Test Q29: To get a stream that fell behind Delta retention running again, set `spark.sql.files.ignoreMissingFiles=true`.
exercises.explain: No. Databricks warns this can silently produce incorrect streaming results. Increase retention or recover/rebuild the stream appropriately.

exercises.q: A stream reading a Delta source stops on Friday. The source's file retention for VACUUM is 7 days. What is the maximum number of whole days the stream can stay stopped and still be sure to catch up (assuming VACUUM runs daily)?
exercises.explain: It must run at least once within the retention window: after more than 7 days, files it needs may be vacuumed. The '2 weeks later' restart in the source example fails.

exercises.q: A Silver stream reading `ecommerce.bronze.events` was paused for a 3-week migration. On restart it fails with a missing-file error.

steps.prompt: What do you check first?

options.text: Source retention settings and DESCRIBE HISTORY for VACUUM runs during the pause
options.fb: Right — compare the pause with retention.

options.text: The watermark delay
options.fb: Watermarks don't delete source files.

options.text: Whether the trigger is AvailableNow
options.fb: Trigger type doesn't affect retention.

steps.prompt: VACUUM with 7-day retention ran weekly. A colleague suggests ignoreMissingFiles=true. Your answer?

options.text: No — it may silently produce incorrect results; recover/rebuild instead
options.fb: Correct — don't suppress a correctness error.

options.text: Yes, the missing files were probably empty
options.fb: You have no evidence of that; data would silently go missing.

options.text: Yes, but only for one run
options.fb: One run is enough to lose data silently.

steps.prompt: How do you prevent it next time?

options.text: Design retention and streaming operations together: longer retention or guarantee runs within the window
options.fb: Yes — a real production operational requirement.

options.text: Delete the checkpoint before every pause
options.fb: That causes reprocessing and duplicates.

options.text: Use complete mode
options.fb: Irrelevant to source retention.

exercises.explain: A stream must run at least once within the source retention window.

exercises.q: A Bronze Delta table used as a streaming source starts receiving UPDATE and DELETE commits. What is the right default thinking?
options: Nothing changes — a Delta source streams row-level changes automatically
A simple Delta source is append-oriented; use Change Data Feed (or deliberately skip change commits) for row-level changes
Switch the sink to complete mode
exercises.explain: A plain Delta streaming source handles appends; non-append commits need care. CDF (`readChangeFeed`) propagates row-level changes; `skipChangeCommits` ignores them (changes not propagated).

exercises.q: Match the Delta-source option to its effect.
pairs: non-append change commits make the stream fail
ignore update/delete commits; changes not propagated
hides missing files — can give silent wrong results
exercises.explain: Pick the behaviour deliberately; never use ignoreMissingFiles as a retention workaround.

exercises.q: Increase the source table's retention so a stopped stream has more time to catch up: set `delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration` to 14 days and `delta.logRetentionDuration` to 30 days on `ecommerce.bronze.events`.
exercises.explain: Increasing retention is one of the two correct fixes (the other: recover/rebuild the stream). It costs storage, so size it to your longest realistic stop.

exercises.q: Delta-source stream fails after a long stop: order the response.
items: Compare stop duration with source retention
Increase retention / guarantee runs within the window
exercises.explain: Diagnose, refuse the silent-wrong-results shortcut, rebuild, then prevent.

exercises.q: Test Q20 + Q21: Why can foreachBatch duplicate external side effects, and what's the solution?
exercises.model: A failed or retried micro-batch may invoke the foreachBatch function again for the same data. External sinks (email, APIs, other databases) don't participate in Spark/Delta transaction semantics, so their effects happen twice. Solution: make the side effects idempotent — e.g. MERGE/upsert by a stable business key and version, or use transactional sink semantics, so that replaying a batch yields the same end state.
rubric: external sinks not transactional with Spark/Delta
exercises.explain: foreachBatch gives power, but sink-side idempotency becomes your responsibility.

exercises.q: Complete the streaming upsert.
exercises.text:
from delta.tables import DeltaTable

def upsert(batch_df, [[batch_id]]):
    target = DeltaTable.[[forName]](spark, "ecommerce.silver.customers")
    (target.alias("t")
        .[[merge]](batch_df.alias("s"), "t.customer_id = s.customer_id")
        .[[whenMatchedUpdateAll]]()
        .whenNotMatchedInsertAll()
        .execute())

query = changes.writeStream.[[foreachBatch]](upsert).option("checkpointLocation", ckpt).start()
exercises.explain: The function receives each micro-batch as a batch DataFrame plus its batch_id; MERGE by key makes it idempotent.

exercises.q: This foreachBatch keeps account balances. After a retry, some balances are doubled. Which line is the bug?
lines: spark.sql(f"UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + {r.amount} WHERE id = {r.id}")
exercises.fix:
-- record each transaction once, keyed by tx_id (replay inserts nothing new)
MERGE INTO ledger t USING batch s ON t.tx_id = s.tx_id
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *
-- balance = SUM(amount) per account, derived from the ledger
exercises.explain: `balance = balance + amount` is not idempotent: a replayed batch applies the increment twice. Key the effect by a stable business id (tx_id) / version so a replay changes nothing. (Collecting to the driver is a second smell.)

exercises.q: `batch_id` alone is a universal business deduplication key for any external sink.
exercises.explain: batch_id can help some sinks recognise replayed batches, but it isn't a business key (and a new checkpoint restarts numbering). The safest design depends on the target system.

exercises.q: Idempotent on replay, or not?

items.text: MERGE by customer_id, update to latest version
overwrite one deterministic partition with the batch's data

exercises.explain: Idempotent = running the same batch twice gives the same end state.

exercises.q: Write a foreachBatch function `merge_counts` that MERGEs `batch_df` into `ecommerce.gold.live_event_counts` on window start and event_type (update all when matched, insert all otherwise), and start the stream from `counts` in update mode with checkpoint `ckpt`.
exercises.solution:
from delta.tables import DeltaTable

def merge_counts(batch_df, batch_id):
    target = DeltaTable.forName(spark, "ecommerce.gold.live_event_counts")
    (target.alias("t")
        .merge(batch_df.alias("s"),
               "t.window_start = s.window.start AND t.event_type = s.event_type")
        .whenMatchedUpdateAll()
        .whenNotMatchedInsertAll()
        .execute())

(counts.writeStream
    .outputMode("update")
    .foreachBatch(merge_counts)
    .option("checkpointLocation", ckpt)
    .start())
exercises.explain: Update mode hands only changed aggregates to the function; MERGE turns them into update-like semantics on the Delta table — what the Delta sink can't do directly.

exercises.q: Which of these can you do inside foreachBatch but NOT directly with a streaming Delta sink?
exercises.explain: foreachBatch exposes each micro-batch as a batch DataFrame, so batch-only operations like MERGE, complex Delta DML or custom sink logic become available.

exercises.q: Test Q30: Input rate permanently exceeds processing rate. What happens?
options: Spark automatically drops the excess input
The checkpoint fixes it on the next restart
exercises.explain: Sustained mismatch → backlog grows, latency grows, and eventually source retention may be exceeded. Q31: a checkpoint doesn't create capacity.

exercises.q: Test Q31: A checkpoint can fix a throughput mismatch between source and pipeline.
exercises.explain: Checkpoint preserves correctness/progress; it doesn't create processing capacity. You need more capacity, a better query, larger batches, less state, better partitioning or less skew.

exercises.q: Source produces 50 MB/s, the pipeline processes 20 MB/s. How many MB of backlog accumulate in 10 minutes?
exercises.explain: Net +30 MB/s × 600 s = **18,000 MB** (~18 GB) — and it keeps growing until capacity or efficiency changes.

exercises.q: Test Q33: One state partition dominates (one task slow, one state partition huge, spill). Likely issue?
options: Key skew (e.g. user_id = 'anonymous' with 70% of events)
exercises.explain: A hot key in a stateful groupBy concentrates state and work in one partition. Streaming partition/key design matters.

exercises.q: Trigger target = 5 s. In each micro-batch 99 partitions finish in 2 s, but one skewed partition takes 30 s. What is the minimum duration (s) of each micro-batch?
exercises.explain: A stage finishes when its slowest task finishes → ≥ **30 s** per batch, 6× the trigger. Backlog grows — the Phase 1 ↔ Phase 5 connection.

exercises.q: Effect of SMALL micro-batches (every 1 s) vs LARGE ones (every 1 min)?

items.text: more frequent commits & storage API calls

exercises.explain: Streaming design balances latency, throughput, cost, state size and correctness.

exercises.q: Which is NOT a valid fix for a sustained backlog?
exercises.explain: A new checkpoint just restarts the query as new (reprocessing, duplicates) — it adds no capacity.

exercises.q: Delta's streaming integration makes small files impossible, so trigger frequency never matters for file layout.
exercises.explain: Tiny micro-batches still create small files (1–3 MB each). OPTIMIZE/predictive optimization can compact later, but choose latency requirements sensibly.

exercises.q: A clickstream aggregation by `user_id` gets slower each day. Spark UI: in every micro-batch, one task takes 40 s while the others take 2 s, with spill. Input rate is stable.

steps.prompt: What is the first hypothesis?

options.text: Key skew: one user_id holds a huge share of events/state
options.fb: Yes — one slow task + one huge state partition = hot key.

options.text: The watermark is too short
options.fb: That drops late data; it doesn't create one slow task.

options.text: The Delta sink doesn't support append
options.fb: It does.

steps.prompt: You find user_id = 'anonymous' is 70% of events. What do you do?

options.text: Rethink the key design (e.g. handle anonymous traffic separately / different grouping key)
options.fb: Right — state partition/key design matters.

options.text: Add more workers only
options.fb: One hot partition stays one task; more workers don't split it.

options.text: Delete the checkpoint
options.fb: Loses state and reprocesses; skew remains.

exercises.explain: Stateful streaming + skew is especially bad: the hot key hurts every batch forever.

exercises.q: Test Q32: Batch durations increase while input rate stays stable. What should you inspect?
exercises.model: State growth (numRowsTotal of stateful operators), checkpoint/state-store overhead, sink and source performance (small files/output overhead, source metadata growth, sink slowdown) and ordinary Spark execution metrics. If state metrics grow endlessly, the watermark/state design is the primary suspect.
exercises.explain: Stable input + growing duration means each batch does more work for the same input — usually state.

exercises.q: lastProgress shows inputRowsPerSecond = 100,000 and processedRowsPerSecond = 40,000 for an hour. Conclusion?
options: Backlog is growing; the pipeline can't keep up
Nothing — CPU is the only reliable metric
exercises.explain: Sustained input > processed → backlog grows. Input 50,000 vs processed 100,000 would mean spare capacity. This ratio is often more useful than cluster CPU.

exercises.q: Walk the production debugging tree for 'streaming latency high'.
exercises.explain: Backlog → slow batch → stage/task metrics → then branch into Spark, state or source/sink factors.

exercises.q: Classify each finding into the tree's branches.

items.text: one task with huge shuffle read
disk spill in the join stage

exercises.explain: Streaming adds state and source/sink factors on top of ordinary Spark performance.

exercises.q: A stream has stopped making progress: no new rows in the sink for two hours. Your manager says 'just restart it'.

steps.prompt: What do you do before restarting?

options.text: Inspect status/lastProgress and the query state first
options.fb: Right — don't restart blindly; preserve the evidence.

options.text: Restart with a new checkpoint to be safe
options.fb: That creates a new query — reprocessing and duplicates.

options.text: Increase the trigger interval
options.fb: Doesn't diagnose anything.

steps.prompt: The query is active and waiting for data. Next check?

options.text: Is the source still producing — are new offsets/files available?
options.fb: Yes — maybe there's simply nothing new.

options.text: Is the watermark too short?
options.fb: Watermarks affect late data, not whether new data is read.

options.text: Is the output mode complete?
options.fb: Not related to progress.

steps.prompt: New files are there, but reading them fails with an authorization error. Likely cause?

options.text: A permission/credential used by the job expired or was revoked
options.fb: One of the classic 'stopped progressing' causes.

options.text: The checkpoint is too large
options.fb: That would slow, not deny access.

options.text: Key skew
options.fb: Skew slows batches; it doesn't cause access errors.

exercises.explain: Checklist: query active? source producing? new offsets? checkpoint corrupted? sink blocked? state batch stuck? executor failure? permission expired? retention violated?

exercises.q: Users report that some late purchase events are missing from the 10-minute revenue windows.

steps.prompt: What do you look at first?

options.text: The missing events' event_time vs the max observed event time and the watermark at their arrival
options.fb: Yes — the event-time chain.

options.text: The checkpoint folder
options.fb: Don't blame the checkpoint first unless evidence points there.

options.text: Cluster CPU
options.fb: Missing late rows are a semantics question first.

steps.prompt: The watermark delay is 5 minutes; the events were 20 minutes behind the max event time. Conclusion?

options.text: They were beyond the watermark and may be dropped — the tolerance is too short for real lateness
options.fb: Correct — measure real lateness and size the watermark.

options.text: Exactly-once is broken
options.fb: Exactly-once is about commits, not lateness.

options.text: The window boundaries are wrong
options.fb: They're assigned by event time correctly.

steps.prompt: What fix keeps late data without unbounded state?

options.text: Increase the watermark to cover realistic lateness (accept more state/latency)
options.fb: That's the explicit latency/state/correctness trade-off.

options.text: Remove the watermark entirely
options.fb: Unbounded state — and append mode wouldn't be allowed.

options.text: Set ignoreMissingFiles=true
options.fb: Unrelated and dangerous.

exercises.explain: Missing late records: event_time → max observed → configured watermark → watermark progress → output mode → window boundaries.

exercises.q: After a cluster failure, the gold customer table and an external CRM both show duplicate entries.

steps.prompt: Which question comes first?

options.text: Is the sink a managed Delta sink, a custom sink or a foreachBatch?
options.fb: Exactly-once only holds where every piece participates.

options.text: Is the trigger interval too short?
options.fb: Doesn't create duplicates.

options.text: Is the watermark too long?
options.fb: Doesn't create duplicates.

steps.prompt: It's a foreachBatch that MERGEs into Delta and POSTs to the CRM. Where do the CRM duplicates come from?

options.text: The retried batch re-ran the non-idempotent POST
options.fb: External side effects aren't covered by Delta transactions.

options.text: Delta's MERGE duplicated rows
options.fb: MERGE by key is idempotent.

options.text: The source can't contain duplicates
options.fb: Sources can — but here the retry explains it.

steps.prompt: But the Delta table has duplicates too. What else do you check?

options.text: Whether the source itself contains duplicates or the checkpoint was reset
options.fb: Both are on the duplicates checklist.

options.text: Whether update mode is enabled
options.fb: Not a duplicate mechanism.

options.text: Whether Photon is on
options.fb: Unrelated.

exercises.explain: Checklist: Delta sink? custom sink? foreachBatch? source duplicates? checkpoint reset? non-idempotent side effect?

exercises.q: State store is huge. Which item is NOT on the 'state store huge' checklist?
exercises.explain: The checklist: number of keys, watermark, window duration, late-data tolerance, join time bounds, dedup horizon, stateful key skew. Output file size belongs to the sink/small-files branch.

exercises.q: Complete the monitoring calls.
exercises.text:
query.[[status]]          # what is it doing right now?
query.[[lastProgress]]    # metrics of the last micro-batch
query.[[recentProgress]]  # recent progress reports
exercises.explain: status = current activity; lastProgress = metrics of the last batch (rates, durations, state, watermark); recentProgress = history.

exercises.q: When batch durations grow while input is stable, and state metrics grow endlessly, the primary suspect is the watermark/state design.
exercises.explain: Stable input + growing state → each batch does more state work. Missing watermark, too long watermark, unbounded key cardinality or a bad stateful join.

exercises.q: Stream stopped making progress: order the checks as in the playbook (mnemonic ON → FED → STUCK → ALLOWED).
items: Is the source still producing / new offsets available?
Is a state batch stuck or an executor failing?
exercises.explain: Start with the cheapest/most obvious (is it even running? is there new data?) before deeper causes; never restart blindly.

exercises.q: Batch durations grow with stable input: order the investigation.
items: Confirm input rate is stable but duration grows
Review watermark / window / join bounds / dedup horizon
Check small files and sink latency
exercises.explain: State is the primary suspect when input is stable; then state-store overhead; then output/sink costs.

exercises.q: Test Q35 (interview): How would you explain Structured Streaming?
exercises.model: Structured Streaming treats an unbounded data source as an incrementally growing table. The developer defines transformations using Spark's DataFrame model, while the engine executes newly available data in micro-batches or supported low-latency modes. Checkpoints track source progress and commits, and state stores preserve intermediate state for aggregations, joins and deduplication. Watermarks bound that state and define lateness tolerance for event-time processing.
rubric: unbounded source as an incrementally growing table
exercises.explain: A strong answer touches model, execution, durability, state and time — in that order.

exercises.q: Lab 1: complete the rate source.
exercises.explain: The rate source produces `timestamp` and an increasing `value` — a synthetic stream without external ingestion complexity.

exercises.q: Match each lab to what it teaches.
exercises.explain: Each lab isolates one engine concept; Lab 4 (windows) and Lab 7 (late data) cover event time.

exercises.q: Order the design questions of the best-practice mental model.
items: EVENT TIME: which timestamp is reality?
LATE DATA: how late can valid records be?
WATERMARK: when can old state go?
CHECKPOINT & RETENTION: durable progress, recoverable source?
exercises.explain: Mnemonic S-E-L-S-W-T-S-C-R. These are not independent choices — each one constrains the next.

exercises.q: Mini-project Gold: from `ecommerce.silver.events`, 20-minute watermark on `event_time`, count events per 5-minute window and `event_type` as `events`, append to `ecommerce.gold.events_5min` with checkpoint `/Volumes/ecommerce/system/events_gold_5min`.
exercises.explain: Stateful windowed aggregation + watermark + append: one final row per window and event type; state evicted after finalization.

exercises.q: Mini-project Silver: stream `ecommerce.bronze.events`, drop rows with NULL `event_id` or `event_time`, write with AvailableNow to `ecommerce.silver.events`, checkpoint `/Volumes/ecommerce/system/bronze_to_silver_events`.
exercises.solution:
bronze = spark.readStream.table("ecommerce.bronze.events")
silver = (
    bronze
        .filter("event_id IS NOT NULL")
        .filter("event_time IS NOT NULL")
)
(
    silver.writeStream
        .trigger(availableNow=True)
        .option("checkpointLocation", "/Volumes/ecommerce/system/bronze_to_silver_events")
        .toTable("ecommerce.silver.events")

exercises.explain: Stateless clean/validate step: only progress is tracked, so AvailableNow on a schedule is perfect.

exercises.q: Mini-project test plan: what do you EXPECT to see?

items.text: very late events beyond the watermark
a normal stream restart with the same checkpoint

exercises.explain: Testing deliberately teaches the semantics: watermark tolerance, checkpoint identity and retention. (Duplicate business events would also pass through — dedup is separate.)

exercises.q: Lab 6 (using a new checkpoint location to see the stream restart as new) is a reasonable quick fix to try in production when a stream misbehaves.
exercises.explain: Only in a sandbox. In production a new checkpoint means a new query: reprocessing, duplicate side effects and lost state.

exercises.q: You want to run the mini-project's Gold query on a serverless job. What must change?
options: Nothing — the default trigger works everywhere
exercises.explain: Serverless notebooks/jobs support AvailableNow (and deprecated Once), not default/time-based triggers. For always-on, use a Lakeflow pipeline in continuous mode.
